alabama.service_animal_def: A service animal is an animal individually trained to do work or perform tasks directly related to a person's disability, including guiding a person who is blind, alerting a person who is deaf or hard of hearing, pulling a wheelchair, assisting with mobility or balance, alerting to seizures or allergens, retrieving items, and helping a person with a psychiatric or neurological disability (for example, interrupting impulsive behavior, reminding the person to take medication, or calming the person during a PTSD anxiety attack). The definition follows the federal ADA regulation (28 C.F.R. 35.104) and covers dogs and, in the public-accommodation context, miniature horses. Trainers and animals in training have the same access rights while training. Ala. Code 21-7-1, 21-7-4 (as amended by Act 2019-478).
alabama.public_access_note: A person with a disability may be accompanied by a service animal in all areas of a public accommodation that the public or customers are normally allowed to enter, including restaurants, stores, hotels, schools, public transportation, and government buildings, with no extra charge and no deposit. When it is not obvious what service the animal provides, staff may ask only the two ADA questions: (1) Is this a service animal required because of a disability? and (2) What work or task has the animal been trained to perform? Staff may not ask about the person's disability or demand proof, certification, or a vest. Alabama goes beyond the ADA by giving trainers and service animals in training the same public access rights, and by naming autism explicitly.
alabama.esa_note: Emotional support animals are NOT service animals under the ADA or Alabama law, because comfort, companionship, and crime deterrence do not count as trained work or tasks. An ESA has no right to enter restaurants, stores, hotels, or other public places in Alabama. In housing, an ESA may qualify as an assistance animal under the federal Fair Housing Act, which is a separate housing rule, not a public-access right.
alabama.misrepresentation_penalty: Knowingly and willfully misrepresenting yourself as using a service animal (or as a trainer of one) is a Class C misdemeanor, with a $100 fine and 100 hours of community service with an organization serving people with disabilities, to be completed within six months; a second or subsequent violation is a Class B misdemeanor with a $100 fine. Ala. Code 21-7-4(h)-(i), Act 2019-478, effective September 1, 2019.
alabama.housing_note: A person with a disability may keep a service animal in a housing accommodation with no extra fee, charge, or deposit, and a landlord may not deny housing because of the service animal. The handler is liable for any damage the animal causes. Ala. Code 21-7-4; Ala. Code Title 24 (Alabama Fair Housing Law) and the federal Fair Housing Act also require reasonable accommodation of assistance animals.
alabama.state_statute: Alabama Code Title 21, Chapter 7 (Rights of Blind and Otherwise Physically Disabled Persons), Ala. Code 21-7-1 through 21-7-9
alabama.agency_name: No state human rights agency in Alabama — ADA complaints go to the U.S. Department of Justice
alabama.state_note: Alabama modernized its law in 2019 (Act 2019-478) to track the ADA, adding criminal penalties for fake service animals, protection for animals in training, and an explicit mention of autism. Public places must post a sign stating service animals are welcome and that misrepresentation is illegal.
alabama.sources: Ala. Code 21-7-1, 21-7-4 (Alabama Legislature, SB10 enrolled, Act 2019-478), Animal Legal & Historical Center Table of State Assistance Animal Laws, Alabama Retail Association summary of Act 2019-478

alaska.service_animal_def: A service animal is a dog or miniature horse individually trained to do work or perform tasks directly related to a person's disability, under 6 AAC 30.610 and the State of Alaska ADA policy. Alaska's criminal statute (AS 11.76.130) uses the older term 'certified service animal,' meaning an animal certified by a school or training facility, but the ADA controls in practice and no certification, ID card, vest, or registration may be demanded. Authorized trainers and animals in training are covered under AS 11.76.133. Alaska's disability definition (AS 18.80.300) expressly includes a condition that might require the use of a service animal.
alaska.public_access_note: A person with a disability may be accompanied by a service animal, without extra charge, in a common carrier, place of public accommodation, or any place open to the general public, including restaurants, stores, hotels, hospitals, government buildings, schools, and public transportation including ferries and the Alaska Marine Highway. Staff may ask only the two ADA questions: (1) Is the dog (or miniature horse) a service animal required because of a disability? and (2) What work or task has it been trained to perform? Alaska goes beyond the ADA by making it a crime to deny access (Class B misdemeanor) and by expressly requiring ride-hailing services to accommodate service animals (AS 28.23.120).
alaska.esa_note: Emotional support animals are NOT service animals under the ADA or Alaska law; animals whose sole function is comfort or emotional support do not qualify. An ESA has no public access rights in Alaska, and Alaska has no state ESA statute. In housing, an ESA may be an assistance animal under the federal Fair Housing Act, with a reasonable accommodation request and supporting documentation if the need is not apparent.
alaska.misrepresentation_penalty: No specific state penalty. Alaska has no statute criminalizing falsely claiming an animal is a service animal (confirmed by the Animal Legal & Historical Center's fraudulent service dog map, which lists Alaska as a state without such a law). What Alaska does criminalize is interfering with a legitimate handler's access: interference under AS 11.76.130 is a Class B misdemeanor (up to 90 days in jail and a fine of up to $2,000), and interfering with training under AS 11.76.133 carries a fine of up to $500.
alaska.housing_note: A landlord may not refuse housing or charge extra fees because of a service animal, and must make reasonable accommodations for service animals and other assistance animals under the Alaska Human Rights Law (AS 18.80.240) and the federal Fair Housing Act. A housing provider may ask for documentation of the disability-related need for an assistance animal only when the disability or need is not apparent.
alaska.state_statute: Alaska Stat. 11.76.130 (Interference with rights of physically or mentally challenged persons), 11.76.133 (Interference with training of a service animal), and AS 18.80.230, 18.80.240 (Alaska Human Rights Law)
alaska.agency_name: Alaska State Commission for Human Rights
alaska.state_note: Alaska's disability definition is broader than the ADA's because it expressly includes a condition that might require a service animal, and its criminal access statute is unusually strong, with jail time for denying access. The older 'certified service animal' wording in the criminal code conflicts with the ADA regulation definition, and the ADA controls.
alaska.sources: AS 11.76.130, AS 11.76.133, AS 18.80.230, AS 18.80.240, 6 AAC 30.610, State of Alaska ADA Compliance Program Service Animal Policy (ADA101), Animal Legal & Historical Center Fraudulent Service Dogs map

arizona.service_animal_def: A service animal is a dog or miniature horse individually trained or in training to do work or perform tasks for the benefit of a person with a disability, including a physical, sensory, psychiatric, intellectual, or other mental disability, with the work or tasks directly related to the disability. Examples include guiding a person who is blind, alerting a person who is deaf, pulling a wheelchair, assisting during a seizure, alerting to allergens, retrieving items, and helping a person with a psychiatric or neurological disability by preventing or interrupting impulsive or destructive behaviors. The crime-deterrent effect of an animal's presence and the provision of emotional support, well-being, comfort, or companionship do NOT count as work or tasks. A.R.S. 11-1024.
arizona.public_access_note: A person or entity operating a public place may not discriminate against a person with a disability who uses a service animal, so the animal must be allowed in restaurants, stores, hotels, public transportation, and government buildings and other public places. Staff may ask only the two ADA questions: (1) Is this a service animal required because of a disability? and (2) What work or task has it been trained to perform? Arizona goes beyond the ADA by giving trainers and animals in training the same public access rights, and by making a violation of the access rule a Class 2 misdemeanor.
arizona.esa_note: Emotional support animals are NOT service animals under Arizona law and have no public access rights; the statute expressly says emotional support, well-being, comfort, and companionship are not work or tasks. In housing, however, Arizona's 2025 law (HB 2068, Chapter 191) defines an 'assistance animal' in A.R.S. 41-1491 to include a trained or untrained animal that provides therapeutic or emotional support, so an ESA can be a reasonable accommodation in housing with reliable documentation of the disability and the need.
arizona.misrepresentation_penalty: Fraudulently misrepresenting an animal as a service animal or service animal in training is subject to a civil penalty of not more than $250 per violation under A.R.S. 11-1024(K). Denying or interfering with access is a separate Class 2 misdemeanor under the same statute.
arizona.housing_note: A landlord must make reasonable accommodations for service animals and assistance animals (including ESAs) under the Arizona Fair Housing Act (A.R.S. 41-1491 et seq.) and the federal Fair Housing Act, and may not charge pet fees or deposits for an assistance animal allowed as an accommodation. The landlord may ask for reliable documentation of the disability and the disability-related need when it is not apparent, and the tenant is liable for damage the animal causes; a 2025 law shields landlords from liability for injuries caused by an assistance animal they allowed as an accommodation.
arizona.state_statute: Arizona Revised Statutes 11-1024 (Service animals; rights of individuals with disabilities) and A.R.S. 41-1491 et seq. (Arizona Fair Housing Act)
arizona.agency_name: Arizona Attorney General, Civil Rights Division
arizona.state_note: Arizona updated its housing law in 2025 (HB 2068, signed May 13, 2025, effective September 26, 2025) to write ESA protections directly into state law, so Arizona renters do not depend only on federal guidance. Arizona also bars counties from charging a dog license fee for a service animal (A.R.S. 11-1008).
arizona.sources: A.R.S. 11-1024 (Arizona Legislature), A.R.S. 41-1491 as amended by HB 2068, Chapter 191 (Arizona Legislature), Arizona Attorney General Civil Rights Guide: Service, Support, and Assistance Animals (2023)

arkansas.service_animal_def: Arkansas defines 'service animal' by reference to the federal ADA regulation, 28 C.F.R. 36.104 (A.C.A. 20-14-311, as updated by Act 268 of 2023): a dog individually trained to do work or perform tasks for the benefit of a person with a disability, with the work or tasks directly related to the disability, including guide work, alerting a person who is deaf, pulling a wheelchair, and other disability-related tasks. Miniature horses are covered under the ADA regulations the state adopts. Service animals in training are covered: a trainer in the act of training a guide, signal, or service dog has the same access rights. A.C.A. 20-14-304, 20-14-308, 20-14-311.
arkansas.public_access_note: Every person with a visual, hearing, or other physical disability has the right to be accompanied by a service animal in or upon all public ways, public places, other public accommodations, and housing accommodations listed in A.C.A. 20-14-303, including restaurants, stores, hotels, lodging, and public transportation, with no extra fee or charge. Staff may ask only the two ADA questions: (1) Is this a service animal required because of a disability? and (2) What work or task has it been trained to perform? Arkansas goes beyond the ADA by giving trainers of service animals in training the same access rights and by setting a Class D felony penalty for killing or seriously injuring a service animal.
arkansas.esa_note: Emotional support animals are NOT service animals under the ADA or Arkansas law and have no public access rights. Arkansas regulates ESAs separately: Act 268 of 2023 (A.C.A. 20-14-1001 et seq.) defines an emotional support animal as one that provides emotional, cognitive, or similar support without needing training, requires sellers and providers of ESA dogs and ESA documentation to give written notice that the animal is not a service animal, and penalizes fraudulently selling an ESA as entitled to service animal rights. In housing, an ESA may be an assistance animal under the federal Fair Housing Act.
arkansas.misrepresentation_penalty: Misrepresenting an animal as a service animal or service animal in training to a person or entity operating a public accommodation carries a civil penalty of up to $250 for each violation under A.C.A. 20-14-310 (Act 1002 of 2019). Separately, knowingly and fraudulently representing an emotional support dog as entitled to service animal rights carries escalating civil penalties under A.C.A. 20-14-1004 (Act 268 of 2023): $500 for a first offense, $1,000 for a second offense, and $2,500 for a third or subsequent offense.
arkansas.housing_note: A person with a disability may keep a service animal in a housing accommodation with no extra fee or charge under A.C.A. 20-14-304, and housing providers must make reasonable accommodations for service animals and assistance animals under the Arkansas Fair Housing Act (A.C.A. 16-123-201 et seq.) and the federal Fair Housing Act. The handler is liable for damage the animal causes to the premises.
arkansas.state_statute: Arkansas Code Title 20, Chapter 14, Subchapter 3, A.C.A. 20-14-304, 20-14-308, 20-14-310, 20-14-311; and Subchapter 10 (Emotional Support Animals), A.C.A. 20-14-1001 et seq.
arkansas.state_note: Arkansas is one of the few states that penalizes ESA fraud as well as service animal fraud, and its 2023 law (Act 268) also puts duties on businesses that sell ESA dogs and on health care providers who write ESA documentation. Arkansas also applies its employment disability protections at a lower threshold of 9 employees.
arkansas.sources: A.C.A. 20-14-304, 20-14-308, 20-14-310, 20-14-311 (FindLaw and Justia 2025 Arkansas Code), Act 1002 of 2019, Act 268 of 2023 (Arkansas Bureau of Legislative Research)

california.service_animal_def: California covers guide dogs, signal dogs, and service dogs. A service dog is a dog individually trained to do work or perform tasks for a person with a disability, including minimal protection work, rescue work, pulling a wheelchair, and fetching dropped items; a signal dog alerts a person who is deaf or hard of hearing to intruders or sounds; a guide dog assists a person who is blind. Miniature horses are covered as service animals under the ADA, which California incorporates. Service dogs in training have the same public access rights when accompanied by a trainer. Cal. Civ. Code 54.1, 54.25; Cal. Penal Code 365.5.
california.public_access_note: A person with a disability has full and equal access to all public accommodations, medical facilities, transportation, and other places open to the public while accompanied by a guide, signal, or service dog, with no extra fee or deposit, and a violation of the ADA is also a violation of California law. Staff may ask only the two ADA questions: (1) Is the dog a service animal required because of a disability? and (2) What work or task has the dog been trained to perform? California goes well beyond the ADA: denying access can bring actual damages of at least $1,000 per offense and up to three times actual damages plus attorney's fees (Civ. Code 54.3), and interfering with access is a misdemeanor with a fine of up to $2,500 (Penal Code 365.5).
california.esa_note: Emotional support animals are NOT service animals under California law and have no right to enter businesses or public places; only trained service animals have that right. In housing, however, a person with a disability may request a reasonable accommodation for an assistance animal, including an ESA, under the California Fair Employment and Housing Act and the federal Fair Housing Act, and the housing provider may ask for reliable documentation if the disability or need is not apparent.
california.misrepresentation_penalty: Knowingly and fraudulently representing yourself as the owner or trainer of a service dog is a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of up to $1,000, up to six months in county jail, or both. Cal. Penal Code 365.7.
california.housing_note: It is a denial of equal access to housing to refuse to lease to a person who uses an assistance dog, and housing providers must make reasonable accommodations for service animals and assistance animals, with no extra fee or pet deposit for the animal. Cal. Civ. Code 54.1; Cal. Gov. Code 12955 (Fair Employment and Housing Act) and the federal Fair Housing Act. The handler is liable for damage the animal causes.
california.state_statute: California Disabled Persons Act, Cal. Civil Code 54-54.8 (especially 54.1, 54.2, 54.3, 54.25); Cal. Penal Code 365.5, 365.6, 365.7
california.legal_aid_name: Legal Aid Foundation of Los Angeles
california.state_note: California is one of the most protective states for service animal handlers: its minimum $1,000 in damages per access denial and its criminal penalties for interference are far stronger than the ADA alone, and the state has a dedicated Disabled Persons Act intake form at the Civil Rights Department. California also has a voluntary local animal-control ID tag program for service animals, but no tag or certification is required.
california.sources: Cal. Civ. Code 54.1, 54.2, 54.3, 54.25; Cal. Penal Code 365.5, 365.6, 365.7; Disability Rights California, Fact Sheet: Service Animals in Business and Public Spaces

colorado.service_animal_def: Colorado defines a service animal by reference to the ADA Title II and III regulations (C.R.S. 24-34-301): a dog or miniature horse individually trained to do work or perform tasks for the benefit of a person with a disability, with the work or task directly related to the disability. The provision of emotional support, well-being, comfort, or companionship does NOT count as work or tasks. No vest, marking, or documentation is required, and a trainer, or a person with a disability accompanied by an animal being trained as a service animal, has the same access rights. C.R.S. 24-34-301, 24-34-803.
colorado.public_access_note: A qualified person with a disability may be accompanied by a service animal in employment, housing, public accommodations, public entity programs and services, public transportation, and other places open to the public, including restaurants, stores, theaters, and hospitals, with no extra charge. Staff may ask only the two ADA questions: (1) Is the dog (or miniature horse) a service animal required because of a disability? and (2) What work or task has it been trained to perform? Colorado goes beyond the ADA by expressly requiring employers to let an employee with a disability keep a service animal with them at all times at work (C.R.S. 24-34-803(3)), and by giving animals in training full access rights.
colorado.esa_note: Emotional support animals are NOT service animals under Colorado law and have no public access rights. In housing, however, Colorado's 2026 law (HB26-1045, effective August 12, 2026) writes ESA protections into the Colorado Anti-Discrimination Act: an 'assistance animal' expressly includes an emotional support animal, and allowing one is presumed to be a reasonable accommodation once the housing provider has had a chance to engage in an interactive process. A provider may ask for reasonable documentation of the disability and need when they are not obvious.
colorado.misrepresentation_penalty: Intentionally misrepresenting an animal as a service animal or service animal in training to obtain rights under C.R.S. 24-34-803 is a petty offense under C.R.S. 18-13-107.7, applying after a prior written or verbal warning and with knowledge the animal is not a service animal; fines are $25 for a first offense, $50 to $200 for a second offense, and $100 to $500 for a third or later offense. Intentionally misrepresenting entitlement to an assistance animal in housing is a civil infraction under C.R.S. 18-13-107.3 with the same fine scale.
colorado.housing_note: A housing provider must make reasonable accommodations for service animals and assistance animals, including ESAs, under the Colorado Anti-Discrimination Act (C.R.S. 24-34-502, 24-34-502.2, as amended by HB26-1045) and the federal Fair Housing Act, and may not charge pet fees or deposits for an assistance animal allowed as an accommodation. Since August 2026, permitting an assistance animal is presumed reasonable, and the mere presence of an assistance animal is not a direct threat or presumed to cause substantial property damage.
colorado.state_statute: Colorado Revised Statutes 24-34-301, 24-34-803, 24-34-804 (Colorado Anti-Discrimination Act); C.R.S. 18-13-107.7 (misrepresentation)
colorado.state_note: Colorado's 2026 law (HB26-1045, signed May 28, 2026, effective August 12, 2026) codified the rescinded federal assistance-animal guidance into state law, so ESA housing rights in Colorado no longer depend on federal enforcement. Colorado also requires a landlord who asks for assistance-animal documentation to give the tenant the Civil Rights Division's form if it is posted online (C.R.S. 24-34-309).

connecticut.service_animal_def: Connecticut defines 'service animal' by reference to the federal ADA regulation, 28 C.F.R. 35.104 (Conn. Gen. Stat. 22-345, as aligned by Public Act 24-18, effective July 1, 2024): a dog individually trained to do work or perform tasks for a person with a disability, with the work or tasks directly related to the disability. The definition also covers an animal in training to become a service animal, and miniature horses are covered under the ADA regulation the state adopts. The older state wording limiting coverage to blind, deaf, or mobility-impaired people was replaced by the 2024 alignment.
connecticut.public_access_note: A person with a disability, or a person training a service animal, may enter any place of public accommodation and ride public transportation with the service animal and keep it with them at all times at no extra charge, as long as the animal is in the person's direct custody and control (Conn. Gen. Stat. 46a-44, 46a-64). Staff may ask only the two ADA questions: (1) Is this a service animal required because of a disability? and (2) What work or task has the animal been trained to perform? Connecticut goes beyond the ADA in that the statute writes those two questions into state law (46a-64), and the owner of a service animal gets a dog license and tag from the town clerk at no fee (22-345).
connecticut.esa_note: Emotional support animals are NOT service animals under Connecticut law or the ADA and have no public access rights. In housing, an ESA may be an assistance animal under the federal Fair Housing Act and Connecticut's fair housing law (Conn. Gen. Stat. 46a-64c), by reasonable accommodation, with documentation if the disability or need is not apparent.
connecticut.misrepresentation_penalty: No specific state penalty. Connecticut has no enacted statute criminalizing misrepresentation of an animal as a service animal; the Connecticut General Assembly's 2014 research report and current guides confirm this, and 2025 bills that would have created such a misdemeanor (Proposed H.B. 5690 and S.B. 1130) died in committee. Do not confuse this with the penalties for denying access: refusing entry is a Class D misdemeanor under 46a-64, and intentionally interfering with a service animal is a Class C misdemeanor under 46a-44(d).
connecticut.housing_note: A housing provider may not discriminate against a person with a disability who uses a service animal, and must make reasonable accommodations for service animals and assistance animals under Conn. Gen. Stat. 46a-64c and the federal Fair Housing Act, with no extra charge for the animal. Violation of 46a-64c is a Class D misdemeanor, punishable by up to 30 days in jail and a fine of up to $250.
connecticut.state_statute: Connecticut General Statutes 46a-44, 46a-64, 46a-64c, and 22-327, 22-345 (definition); Public Act 24-18 (2024)
connecticut.agency_name: Connecticut Commission on Human Rights and Opportunities
connecticut.state_note: Connecticut aligned its service animal definition with the ADA only in 2024 (Public Act 24-18, effective July 1, 2024), which also removed the old requirement that a service animal wear a harness or orange leash and collar. Complaints to the Commission on Human Rights and Opportunities must be filed within 300 days of the discriminatory act.
connecticut.sources: Conn. Gen. Stat. 46a-44, 46a-64, 46a-64c, 22-345 (Justia 2025 Connecticut General Statutes); Connecticut General Assembly Research Report 2014-R-0025; Public Act 24-18

delaware.service_animal_def: A service animal is a dog individually trained to do work or perform tasks for the benefit of a person with a disability, including a physical, sensory, psychiatric, intellectual, or other mental disability (6 Del. C. 4502(28), updated in 2018 to align with the ADA). The state definition names dogs only; miniature horses are covered as service animals under the ADA itself. A person training a service animal has the same public access rights. The White Cane Law (16 Del. C. 9501-9506) separately protects guide dogs for people who are blind or visually impaired.
delaware.public_access_note: A place of public accommodation may not deny access to a person with a disability accompanied by a service animal, or to a person training a service animal, under the Delaware Equal Accommodations Law (6 Del. C. 4504(a)(3)), so the animal must be allowed in restaurants, stores, hotels, theaters, and other public places. Staff may ask only the two ADA questions: (1) Is this a service animal required because of a disability? and (2) What work or task has the animal been trained to perform? Delaware goes beyond the ADA by extending access rights to trainers and by making it a felony-level offense to kill or steal a service dog, with strong criminal penalties for interfering with, injuring, or stealing one (16 Del. C. 3056F).
delaware.esa_note: Emotional support animals are NOT service animals under Delaware law and have no public access rights. In housing, Delaware law uses the broader term 'support animal' (6 Del. C. 4602): an animal other than a service animal that does work, performs tasks, provides assistance, or provides therapeutic emotional support for a person with a disability, which can qualify for a reasonable accommodation under the Delaware Fair Housing Act and the federal Fair Housing Act.
delaware.misrepresentation_penalty: No specific state penalty. Delaware has no enacted penalty for misrepresenting a pet as a service animal. Senate Bill 219 (2024) would have created one (a $500 civil penalty for a first offense and an unclassified misdemeanor for a second or later offense, under proposed 6 Del. C. 4514 and 4621), but it did not pass and is not law.
delaware.housing_note: A housing provider must make reasonable accommodations for assistance animals, including service animals and support animals, under the Delaware Fair Housing Act (6 Del. C. Chapter 46, especially 4603A) and the federal Fair Housing Act, and may not charge pet fees or deposits for an assistance animal allowed as an accommodation. The provider may request disability-related information when the disability or the need for the animal is not apparent.
delaware.state_statute: Delaware Equal Accommodations Law, 6 Del. C. Chapter 45 (especially 4502, 4504); White Cane Law, 16 Del. C. Chapter 95; Delaware Fair Housing Act, 6 Del. C. Chapter 46
delaware.agency_name: Delaware Division of Human and Civil Rights
delaware.state_note: Delaware's protections are spread across three chapters of the Code, and its 2018 update to the Equal Accommodations Law broadened the definition from physical disabilities only to all disabilities, including psychiatric and intellectual disabilities. The Division of Human and Civil Rights also administers Delaware's Fair Housing and Equal Accommodations laws, and the Community Legal Aid Society is Delaware's Protection and Advocacy agency for people with disabilities.
delaware.sources: 6 Del. C. 4502, 4504, 4602, 4603A; 16 Del. C. 9502, 3056F; Delaware General Assembly SB 219 (152nd General Assembly, 2024, did not pass); Delaware Division of Human and Civil Rights

florida.service_animal_def: A service animal is an animal trained to do work or perform tasks for a person with a disability, including a physical, sensory, psychiatric, intellectual, or other mental disability, with the work or tasks directly related to the disability, including guiding a person who is blind, alerting a person who is deaf, pulling a wheelchair, assisting with mobility or balance, alerting and protecting a person having a seizure, retrieving objects, alerting to allergens, and helping a person with a psychiatric or neurological disability. For public accommodations, employment, and housing under the statute, the term is limited to a dog or miniature horse. The crime-deterrent effect of an animal's presence and the provision of emotional support, well-being, comfort, or companionship do NOT count as work or tasks. Trainers and animals in training have the same rights. Fla. Stat. 413.08(1)(d), (8).
florida.public_access_note: A person with a disability is entitled to full and equal accommodations in all public accommodations and has the right to be accompanied by a service animal in all areas the public or customers are normally permitted to occupy, including restaurants, stores, hotels, lodging, public transportation, and government buildings. Staff may ask only the two ADA questions: (1) Is this a service animal required because of a disability? and (2) What work or task has it been trained to perform? A business may not ask about the nature or extent of the disability or require documentation that the animal is trained. Florida goes beyond the ADA by making denial of access a second-degree misdemeanor with mandatory community service, and by covering trainers and animals in training in the same statute.
florida.esa_note: Emotional support animals are NOT service animals under Florida law and have no public access rights; the statute expressly excludes emotional support, well-being, comfort, and companionship from the definition of work or tasks. In housing, an ESA may be an assistance animal under the Florida Fair Housing Act and the federal Fair Housing Act, by reasonable accommodation, and Florida law (Fla. Stat. 760.27) sets documentation rules for housing providers, including that an ESA letter must come from a health care practitioner with knowledge of the person's disability.
florida.misrepresentation_penalty: Knowingly and willfully misrepresenting yourself, through conduct or verbal or written notice, as using a service animal and being qualified to use one, or as a trainer of a service animal, is a misdemeanor of the second degree, punishable by a fine of up to $500, up to 60 days in jail, and 30 hours of community service for an organization serving people with disabilities, to be completed within six months. Fla. Stat. 413.08(9).
florida.housing_note: A housing provider may not discriminate against a person with a disability who uses a service animal, and must permit the service animal with no extra charge; a provider who discriminates in housing commits a misdemeanor of the second degree under Fla. Stat. 413.08(6)-(7). Assistance animals, including ESAs, must be reasonably accommodated under the Florida Fair Housing Act (Fla. Stat. 760.23) and the federal Fair Housing Act, with no pet deposit or fee for the animal. The handler is liable for damage the animal causes if the provider regularly charges nondisabled people for pet damage.
florida.state_statute: Florida Statutes 413.08 (Rights and responsibilities of an individual with a disability; use of a service animal) and 413.081 (Interference with or injury to a service animal)
florida.state_note: Florida is unusual in putting public access, housing, employment, trainer rights, and the misrepresentation penalty all in one statute (413.08), and it pairs that with felony-level penalties for intentionally harming a service animal under 413.081. Florida also requires public accommodations to post no extra charge for service animals and expressly includes miniature horses alongside dogs.

georgia.service_animal_def: Note: Georgia rewrote this law in 2026. Under the pre-2026 text (O.C.G.A. 30-4-1, 30-4-2), a 'service dog' was a dog trained by a school for the blind, deaf, or physically disabled, and state protection covered only blind, visually disabled, physically disabled, and deaf people, not psychiatric or intellectual disabilities. House Bill 668, the 'Mara Jade Act' (reported as Act 440, effective July 1, 2026), rewrote the definition to track the federal ADA rules: a dog individually trained to perform tasks directly related to a person's physical or mental disability, with emotional support expressly excluded, and anyone may train a service dog.
georgia.public_access_note: Blind, visually disabled, physically disabled, and deaf people are entitled to full and equal accommodations in all public places while accompanied by a guide dog or service dog, including restaurants, stores, hotels, public transportation, and government buildings, with no extra charge, and the handler is liable for damage the dog causes (O.C.G.A. 30-4-2). Staff may ask only the two ADA questions: (1) Is this a service animal required because of a disability? and (2) What work or task has it been trained to perform? Georgia's state statute is narrower than the ADA because it does not name psychiatric or intellectual disabilities, so psychiatric service dog handlers rely on the federal ADA for state-law gaps; the 2026 rewrite (HB 668) is reported to close that gap.
georgia.esa_note: Emotional support animals are NOT service animals under Georgia law or the ADA and have no public access rights; the 2026 definition expressly writes emotional support out of the service animal definition. In housing, an ESA may be an assistance animal under the Georgia Fair Housing Law (O.C.G.A. 28-3-200 et seq.) and the federal Fair Housing Act, by reasonable accommodation with supporting documentation if the need is not apparent.
georgia.misrepresentation_penalty: As of July 1, 2026, deliberately misrepresenting yourself as qualified to use a service dog (or as a service dog trainer) to obtain accommodations or rights is a misdemeanor of a high and aggravated nature under O.C.G.A. 30-4-4(b) as amended by HB 668, the 'Mara Jade Act': a fine of up to $2,000, up to 30 days of confinement, or both.
georgia.housing_note: A person with a disability may keep a service dog in housing with no extra charge under O.C.G.A. 30-4-2, and housing providers must make reasonable accommodations for service animals and assistance animals under the Georgia Fair Housing Law and the federal Fair Housing Act, with no pet deposit or fee for the animal. Denying or interfering with these rights is a misdemeanor of a high and aggravated nature under O.C.G.A. 30-4-4, with a fine of up to $2,000, up to 30 days in jail, or both.
georgia.state_statute: Official Code of Georgia Annotated Title 30, Chapter 4, O.C.G.A. 30-4-1 through 30-4-4 (Rights of Persons with Visual Disabilities and Deaf Persons), as amended by HB 668 (2025-2026, the 'Mara Jade Act')
georgia.state_note: Georgia's 2026 overhaul (HB 668) is the biggest recent change in this batch: it modernized a narrow, school-trained-dog statute into an ADA-style definition, added the misrepresentation penalty, and strengthened penalties for harming a service dog. Georgia also has a dedicated harassment statute for assistance dogs (O.C.G.A. 16-11-107.1), with at least 90 days in jail or a fine of up to $500 for a first offense.
georgia.sources: O.C.G.A. 30-4-1, 30-4-2, 30-4-4 (FindLaw, current as of March 28, 2024), O.C.G.A. 16-11-107.1; HB 668 (2025-2026) as summarized in 2026 legal updates, Georgia Commission on Equal Opportunity

hawaii.service_animal_def: A service animal is any dog individually trained to do work or perform tasks for a person with a disability, including a physical, sensory, psychiatric, intellectual, or other mental disability (HRS 347-2.5). Other species are not service animals. The work or tasks must relate directly to the disability; crime deterrence, emotional support, comfort, or companionship do not count. Hawaii is the only state whose public-accommodation law does not extend access rights to service animals in training.
hawaii.public_access_note: Under HRS 347-13, a person with a disability has full and equal access to common carriers, hotels and lodging, and places of public accommodation, amusement, or resort, accompanied by a service animal at no extra charge, and is liable for any damage the animal causes. A business may ask only the two ADA questions — whether the animal is required because of a disability and what work or task it has been trained to perform — and may not demand proof of certification or training. Hawaii goes beyond the ADA by allowing a fine of up to $1,000 for violating HRS 347-13 (HRS 347-14) and a civil claim for three times actual damages or $1,000, whichever is greater, plus costs and attorney fees (HRS 347-13.5).
hawaii.esa_note: Emotional support animals are not service animals under the ADA or Hawaii law, and they have no public-access rights in restaurants, stores, hotels, or transport. In housing, however, Hawaii law treats ESAs as assistance animals (see housing note).
hawaii.misrepresentation_penalty: Civil penalty under HRS 347-2.6: knowingly misrepresenting an animal as a service animal carries a fine of $100 to $250 for a first violation and $500 or more for a second and each later violation, on clear and convincing evidence.
hawaii.housing_note: Under HRS chapter 515, including HRS 515-3(a)(9) as amended by Act 154 (2022), a person with a disability may request an assistance animal — including an emotional support animal, trained or untrained, and not limited to dogs — as a reasonable accommodation to a no-pets rule. If the disability or need is not obvious, the housing provider may ask for verification from a treating health care professional, mental health professional, or social worker, but may not demand a diagnosis, medical records, or proof of training, and may not charge a pet deposit, pet rent, or extra fee for the animal.
hawaii.state_statute: Hawaii Revised Statutes Chapter 347, sections 347-2.5, 347-2.6, 347-13, 347-13.5 and 347-14; HRS Chapter 489 (public accommodations) and HRS Chapter 515 (housing)
hawaii.state_note: Hawaii is the only rabies-free state, so strict animal quarantine rules apply even to service animals entering the islands, and Hawaii is the only state that does not give service animals in training public-access rights under state law.
hawaii.sources: HRS 347-2.5, HRS 347-2.6, HRS 347-13, HRS 347-13.5, HRS 347-14, HRS 515-3, Hawaii Civil Rights Commission assistance-animals fact sheet, labor.hawaii.gov/hcrc

idaho.service_animal_def: A service dog is a dog individually trained to do work or perform tasks for a person with a disability, including a physical, sensory, psychiatric, intellectual, or other mental disability, with the work or tasks directly related to the disability (Idaho Code 56-701A(5)). Other species, wild or domestic, trained or untrained, are not service animals. Service dogs in training are covered: a person with a disability training or socializing a dog, and a non-disabled trainer with an identification card from a recognized service-dog school or disability organization, may bring the dog into public places.
idaho.public_access_note: Under Idaho Code 56-704 and 56-704A, a person with a disability may be accompanied by a service dog in all places of public accommodation, including restaurants, hotels, stores, theaters, common carriers, and other places the public is invited, with no extra charge or deposit, and is liable for any damage the dog causes. A business may ask only the two ADA questions — whether the dog is required because of a disability and what task it performs — and may not demand certification, identification, or proof of training. An animal may be excluded only if it is out of control or not housebroken, or poses a direct threat to health or safety.
idaho.esa_note: Emotional support animals are not service animals under Idaho law or the ADA and have no public-access rights; comfort, emotional support, or companionship alone do not count as qualifying work. ESAs may be protected in housing only as assistance animals under the federal Fair Housing Act and Idaho fair housing law.
idaho.misrepresentation_penalty: Misdemeanor under Idaho Code 56-704B (effective July 1, 2018): knowingly and intentionally misrepresenting a dog as a service animal or service animal in training to obtain rights or privileges, including by using a vest, tag, or harness, with a fine of up to $500 for a first offense. A separate, older statute, Idaho Code 18-5811A, makes it a misdemeanor to use an assistance animal or service dog to falsely claim disability benefits or treatment.
idaho.housing_note: Under the Idaho Human Rights Act and the federal Fair Housing Act, a housing provider must make a reasonable accommodation for a service animal or other assistance animal needed because of a disability, including waiving a no-pets rule, and may not charge a pet deposit or extra fee for the animal, though the tenant is liable for damage it causes. A provider may ask for reliable documentation of the disability-related need when it is not obvious.
idaho.state_statute: Idaho Code Title 56, Chapter 7, sections 56-701A, 56-703, 56-704, 56-704A, 56-704B, 56-706; Idaho Code 18-5811A
idaho.state_note: Idaho is one of the states that expressly extends public-access rights to service dogs in training, including owner-trainers, and it has two overlapping misrepresentation statutes (56-704B and 18-5811A). Interfering with a service animal's access rights is a misdemeanor under Idaho Code 56-706.
idaho.sources: Idaho Code 56-701A, 56-704, 56-704A, 56-704B, 56-706, Idaho Code 18-5811A, Idaho Human Rights Commission disability page, humanrights.idaho.gov

illinois.service_animal_def: Under 720 ILCS 5/48-8, a service animal is a dog or miniature horse trained or being trained as a hearing animal, guide animal, assistance animal, seizure alert animal, mobility animal, psychiatric service animal, autism service animal, or an animal trained for any other physical, mental, or intellectual disability. This is broader than the ADA in two ways: it includes miniature horses (subject to a four-factor reasonable-accommodation assessment) and animals still being trained.
illinois.public_access_note: A person with a disability accompanied by a service animal, and a trainer accompanied by a service animal in training, may not be denied entry to or use of any public place of accommodation under 720 ILCS 5/48-8 and the Illinois Human Rights Act (775 ILCS 5), including restaurants, stores, hotels, public transport, and government buildings. A business may ask only the two ADA questions — whether the animal is required because of a disability and what work or task it performs — and may not demand documentation, certification, or a demonstration, or charge an extra fee. Illinois also requires public swimming facilities to admit a service dog trained to perform a specific task in the water unless it poses a direct threat.
illinois.esa_note: Emotional support animals are not service animals under Illinois law or the ADA and have no public-access rights; only task-trained service animals (including psychiatric service animals) must be admitted. ESAs may be protected in housing only as assistance animals under the federal Fair Housing Act and the Illinois Human Rights Act.
illinois.misrepresentation_penalty: No specific state penalty for falsely claiming an animal is a service animal. Bills to create one (for example, a petty offense for a knowingly false claim) have been introduced but not enacted. The Class C misdemeanor in 720 ILCS 5/48-8(b) punishes a business that knowingly denies access to a person with a service animal, not a person who fakes one.
illinois.housing_note: Under the Illinois Human Rights Act (775 ILCS 5, Article 3) and the federal Fair Housing Act, a housing provider must make a reasonable accommodation for a service animal or other assistance animal needed because of a disability, including waiving a no-pets rule, and may not charge a pet deposit or extra fee for the animal, though the tenant is liable for damage it causes. A provider may ask for reliable documentation of the disability-related need when it is not obvious.
illinois.state_statute: 720 ILCS 5/48-8 (Service Animal Access Act); Illinois Human Rights Act, 775 ILCS 5; White Cane Law, 775 ILCS 30; Assistance Animal Damages Act, 740 ILCS 13
illinois.state_note: Illinois defines service animals more broadly than the ADA — dogs and miniature horses, including animals in training — and makes knowingly denying access a Class C misdemeanor (up to 30 days in jail and a fine up to $1,500). Prairie State Legal Services serves northern and central Illinois; Land of Lincoln Legal Aid serves southern Illinois.
illinois.sources: 720 ILCS 5/48-8, 775 ILCS 5, 775 ILCS 30, Illinois Department of Human Rights disability rights and public accommodation pages, ilga.gov

indiana.service_animal_def: Under IC 16-32-3-1.5, as amended in 2023, and the newer Service Animals chapter IC 16-32-3.5, a service animal is a dog or miniature horse individually trained to do work or perform tasks for a person with a disability, including as a hearing, guide, assistance, seizure alert, mobility, psychiatric service, or autism service animal. The tasks must be directly related to the disability. Service animal trainers engaged in training have the same public-access rights.
indiana.public_access_note: A person with a physical or mental disability is entitled to be accompanied by a service animal in any public accommodation, including restaurants, stores, hotels, theaters, transportation, and government buildings, without an extra charge, and is liable for any damage the animal causes (IC 16-32-3-2; IC 16-32-3.5). A business may ask only the two ADA questions — whether the animal is required because of a disability and what work or task it is trained to perform — and may not require proof of certification, training, or licensing (IC 16-32-3.5-9). An animal may be excluded only if it is out of control or not housebroken.
indiana.esa_note: Emotional support animals are not service animals under Indiana law or the ADA and have no public-access rights. Indiana does, however, regulate ESAs in housing: knowingly misrepresenting an animal as an emotional support animal in housing, including fitting a non-support animal with a harness, collar, vest, or sign, is a Class A infraction under IC 22-9-7-12.
indiana.misrepresentation_penalty: No specific state penalty for falsely claiming a service animal in public places — Indiana has no service-dog fraud law for public access. The only misrepresentation offense is in housing: falsely claiming an emotional support animal is a Class A infraction under IC 22-9-7-12. Refusing access to, or charging a fee because of, a service animal is a Class C infraction under IC 16-32-3-2(b).
indiana.housing_note: Under the Indiana Fair Housing Act and the federal Fair Housing Act, a housing provider must make a reasonable accommodation for a service animal or emotional support animal needed because of a disability, including waiving a no-pets rule, and may not charge a pet deposit or extra fee for the animal, though the tenant is liable for damage it causes. A provider may ask for reliable documentation of the disability-related need when it is not obvious, and falsifying that documentation can be a Class A infraction under IC 22-9-7-12.
indiana.state_statute: Indiana Code 16-32-3 (White Cane Law) and 16-32-3.5 (Service Animals, enacted 2023 by HEA 1354); IC 22-9-7-12 (emotional support animals in housing)
indiana.state_note: Indiana modernized its law in 2023 (HEA 1354, IC 16-32-3.5), aligning the definition with the ADA and adding the ban on demanding proof of certification. Indiana also has some of the toughest penalties for harming or interfering with a service animal: a Class A misdemeanor, rising to a Level 6 felony if the animal suffers permanent disfigurement, loss of consciousness, serious organ damage, or death (IC 35-46-3-11.5).
indiana.sources: IC 16-32-3-1.5, IC 16-32-3-2, IC 16-32-3.5, IC 22-9-7-12, IC 35-46-3-11.5, Indiana Civil Rights Commission, in.gov/icrc

iowa.service_animal_def: Under Iowa Code 216C.1A, a service animal is a dog or miniature horse as defined in the ADA Title II and Title III regulations — individually trained to do work or perform tasks for a person with a disability, with the tasks directly related to the disability. Service animals in training are covered alongside trained service animals.
iowa.public_access_note: Under Iowa Code 216C.11(1), a person with a disability, a person assisting one by controlling a service animal, or a person training a service animal has the right to be accompanied by the animal, under control, in the places listed in Iowa Code 216C.3 and 216C.4, including streets, sidewalks, public buildings, common carriers, hotels and lodging, eating places, and other places of public accommodation, amusement, or resort, with no extra charge, and is liable for damage the animal causes. A business may ask only the two ADA questions — whether the animal is required because of a disability and what task it performs — and may not demand documentation or proof of training. Knowingly denying or interfering with this right is a simple misdemeanor under 216C.11(2).
iowa.esa_note: Emotional support animals are not service animals under Iowa law or the ADA and have no public-access rights; comfort, emotional support, or companionship alone do not count as qualifying work. ESAs may be protected in housing only as assistance animals under the federal Fair Housing Act and the Iowa Civil Rights Act.
iowa.misrepresentation_penalty: Simple misdemeanor under Iowa Code 216C.11(3), as amended by 2025 Acts, chapter 111 (HF 615), effective July 1, 2025: intentionally misrepresenting an animal as a service animal or service-animal-in-training to obtain rights or privileges under state or federal law. A simple misdemeanor carries up to 30 days in jail and a fine of $105 to $855 (Iowa Code 903.1). The 2025 amendment removed the earlier requirement that the person first have received a warning.
iowa.housing_note: Under the Iowa Civil Rights Act (Iowa Code chapter 216) and the federal Fair Housing Act, a housing provider must make a reasonable accommodation for a service animal or other assistance animal needed because of a disability, including waiving a no-pets rule, and may not charge a pet deposit or extra fee for the animal, though the tenant is liable for damage it causes. A provider may ask for reliable documentation of the disability-related need when it is not obvious.
iowa.state_statute: Iowa Code Chapter 216C (Rights of Persons with Disabilities), sections 216C.1A, 216C.3, 216C.4, and 216C.11
iowa.agency_name: Iowa Office of Civil Rights (Iowa Civil Rights Commission)
iowa.state_note: Iowa has actively updated its law in recent years — 2019, 2024, and 2025 — and the 2025 change made misrepresentation easier to prosecute by dropping the prior-warning requirement. In 2024 the Iowa Civil Rights Commission was converted to an advisory panel inside the Iowa Office of Civil Rights, which continues to enforce the Iowa Civil Rights Act.
iowa.sources: Iowa Code 216C.1A, 216C.3, 216C.4, 216C.11, Iowa Code 903.1, 2025 Acts chapter 111 (HF 615), legis.iowa.gov, icrc.iowa.gov

kansas.service_animal_def: Under K.S.A. 39-1113, an assistance dog is a guide dog, hearing assistance dog, or service dog — a dog specially selected, trained, and tested to guide a person who is legally blind, alert a person who is deaf or hard of hearing to specific sounds, or perform tasks for a person with a disability such as pulling a wheelchair, lending balance support, picking up dropped objects, or helping in or avoiding a medical crisis. The presence of a dog for comfort, protection, or personal defense does not qualify it as an assistance dog. Kansas also recognizes a separate category, a professional therapy dog, trained to provide specific physical or therapeutic functions under a qualified handler as part of that handler's profession.
kansas.public_access_note: Under the Kansas White Cane Law (K.S.A. 39-1101 through 39-1113), persons with disabilities have the same right as others to the full and free use of streets, sidewalks, public buildings, public facilities, and other public places, and to full and equal accommodations of common carriers, hotels, lodging places, places of public accommodation, amusement or resort, and food service establishments, accompanied by an assistance dog at no extra charge, and are liable for damage the dog causes. A business may ask only the two ADA questions — whether the dog is required because of a disability and what task it performs — and may not demand documentation; if a question arises, the person with a disability may choose to show an identification card or letter, which must be promptly returned (K.S.A. 39-1111). Professional therapy dogs also have public-access rights in the places listed in K.S.A. 39-1110.
kansas.esa_note: Emotional support animals are not assistance dogs under Kansas law — a dog kept for comfort does not qualify (K.S.A. 39-1113) — and they have no public-access rights. Kansas has no state ESA statute; ESAs may be protected in housing only as assistance animals under the federal Fair Housing Act and the Kansas Act Against Discrimination.
kansas.misrepresentation_penalty: Class A nonperson misdemeanor under K.S.A. 39-1112: falsely claiming the right to be accompanied by an assistance dog or professional therapy dog in a covered place, or falsely claiming a disability to acquire an assistance dog. A Class A nonperson misdemeanor carries up to 1 year in county jail, a fine up to $2,500, or both (K.S.A. 21-6602, 21-6611).
kansas.housing_note: Under K.S.A. 39-1102, 39-1107, and 39-1108, a person with a disability has the right to be accompanied by a service dog in the acquisition and use of rental housing and in the purchase and use of residential housing, with no extra charge for the dog, and is liable for damage the dog causes. Under the Kansas Act Against Discrimination and the federal Fair Housing Act, a housing provider must also reasonably accommodate other assistance animals needed because of a disability, with no pet deposit or extra fee for the animal.
kansas.state_statute: Kansas White Cane Law / Rights of Persons with Disabilities, K.S.A. 39-1101 through 39-1113; K.S.A. 39-1112 (misrepresentation)
kansas.state_note: Kansas has one of the toughest misrepresentation penalties in the country (up to a year in jail and $2,500), and it is unusual in giving public-access rights to professional therapy dogs working with a qualified handler. Note that the Kansas Human Rights Commission enforces the Kansas Act Against Discrimination, not the White Cane Law itself, whose violations are criminal misdemeanors.

kentucky.service_animal_def: Kentucky uses the term assistance dog (KRS 258.500): a dog individually trained to do work or perform tasks for a person with disabilities, considered a service animal under the ADA. The definition is limited to dogs. A trainer of an assistance dog is also covered and must carry identification verifying trainer status.
kentucky.public_access_note: Under KRS 258.500, a person with an assistance dog may not be denied accommodations at hotels, motels, restaurants, or eating establishments; is entitled to full and equal accommodations on all public transportation with no extra fare, and the dog must not occupy a seat or endanger public safety; and has access to all public buildings and elevators. A business may ask only the two questions codified in KRS 258.500(13) — whether the dog is an assistance dog and what tasks it performs — and may not demand proof of certification, training, or licensing. Assistance dogs are exempt from state and local licensing fees, and no one may willfully or maliciously interfere with the dog or its user.
kentucky.esa_note: Kentucky law expressly defines an emotional support animal as a companion animal that may provide support to alleviate symptoms of a disability but has not been individually trained to do work or perform tasks — and it is explicitly not a service animal under the ADA (KRS 258.500, as amended by HB 335 in 2024). ESAs have no public-access rights in Kentucky, but may be protected in housing as assistance animals (see housing note).
kentucky.misrepresentation_penalty: Fine up to $1,000 under KRS 258.991 for misrepresenting a dog as an assistance dog to gain an accommodation. Separately, in housing, knowingly misrepresenting a disability or need, falsifying documentation, or fitting a non-assistance animal with a harness, collar, vest, or sign carries a fine up to $1,000 under KRS 383.085.
kentucky.housing_note: Under KRS 258.500(6) and KRS 383.085, a person with a disability may keep an assistance dog as a tenant in an apartment or public lodging and may request a reasonable accommodation to keep an assistance animal in a dwelling, with no pet deposit or extra fee for the animal, though the tenant is liable for damage it causes. A housing provider may ask for reliable documentation of the disability-related need when it is not obvious, including proof of a therapeutic relationship with a licensed Kentucky clinician; fee-based online documentation without a face-to-face consultation does not count.
kentucky.state_statute: Kentucky Revised Statutes 258.500 (assistance dogs) and 258.991 (penalties); KRS 383.085 (assistance animals in housing); KRS Chapter 344 (Kentucky Civil Rights Act)
kentucky.state_note: Kentucky substantially updated its law in 2024 (HB 335, effective July 15, 2024), adding formal definitions of assistance dog, emotional support animal, and therapeutic relationship, codifying the two permissible questions, and adding the misrepresentation penalties. Kentucky has no single statewide legal aid program — four regional programs divide the state; Legal Aid of the Bluegrass serves central and northern Kentucky.
kentucky.sources: KRS 258.500, KRS 258.991, KRS 383.085, KRS Chapter 344, Kentucky Commission on Human Rights, kchr.ky.gov

louisiana.service_animal_def: Under La. R.S. 46:1952, a service dog is a dog trained or being trained to do work or perform a task for a person with a disability, including as a hearing dog, guide dog, seizure alert dog, mobility dog, autism service dog, a dog providing assistance during a medical crisis, or a dog assisting persons, including veterans, with traumatic brain injury or post-traumatic stress disorder. The definition covers dogs in training and does not mention miniature horses.
louisiana.public_access_note: Under the Louisiana White Cane Law (La. R.S. 46:1951-1959), a person with a disability has the same right as others to public streets, buildings, and public places, and full and equal access to common carriers, educational institutions, hotels, restaurants, theaters, and other places the public is invited, accompanied by a service dog at no extra charge, and is liable for damage the dog causes (La. R.S. 46:1953). A business may ask only the two ADA questions — whether the dog is required because of a disability and what work or task it performs — and may not ask about the nature or extent of the disability or require proof of certification, training, or licensing. A dog may be removed only if it is out of control and the handler does not control it, or it is not housebroken.
louisiana.esa_note: Emotional support animals are not service animals under Louisiana law or the ADA and have no public-access rights. Louisiana's Support and Service Animal Integrity Act (La. R.S. 46:1971-1978, effective August 1, 2024) tightened ESA documentation in housing: an ESA letter must come from a licensed health care provider with a real therapeutic relationship, and online-only or fee-based letters without an in-person or telehealth evaluation do not qualify.
louisiana.misrepresentation_penalty: Escalating fines under La. R.S. 46:1975: knowingly misrepresenting an animal as a service animal or service animal in training carries a fine up to $500 for a first offense, up to $1,000 for a second offense, and up to $2,500 for a third and each later offense.
louisiana.housing_note: Under La. R.S. 46:1954, persons with disabilities have full and equal access to housing accommodations with a service dog, with no extra charge for the dog, and are liable for damage it causes. Under the federal Fair Housing Act, the Louisiana fair housing law, and the Support and Service Animal Integrity Act, a housing provider must also reasonably accommodate an emotional support animal needed because of a disability, with no pet deposit or extra fee for the animal, and may ask for reliable documentation of the disability-related need when it is not obvious.
louisiana.state_statute: Louisiana White Cane Law, La. R.S. 46:1951-1959; Support and Service Animal Integrity Act, La. R.S. 46:1971-1978
louisiana.state_note: Louisiana's 2024 Support and Service Animal Integrity Act is one of the newest and most detailed service-animal fraud laws in the country, with escalating fines and strict ESA documentation rules. Southeast Louisiana Legal Services serves 22 parishes in southeast Louisiana; Acadiana Legal Service Corporation serves the rest of the state.

maine.service_animal_def: Maine has a two-part definition in 5 M.R.S. 4553(9-E). For public accommodations (subchapter 5), a service animal is a dog individually trained to do work or perform tasks for a person with a disability, including a physical, sensory, psychiatric, intellectual, or other mental disability; other species are not service animals, and crime deterrence, emotional support, well-being, comfort, or companionship do not count as work or tasks. For housing (subchapter 4), the definition is broader: an animal determined necessary to mitigate a physical or mental disability by a physician, psychologist, physician assistant, nurse practitioner, or licensed social worker, or an animal individually trained to do disability-related work or tasks.
maine.public_access_note: Under 5 M.R.S. 4592(8) and the White Cane Law, 17 M.R.S. 1312, a person with a disability has the right to be accompanied by a service animal in all places of public accommodation, including restaurants, stores, hotels, theaters, and public transportation, with no fee or security deposit required, and is liable for damage the animal causes. A business may ask only the two ADA questions — whether the animal is required because of a disability and what work or task it performs — and may not demand documentation or proof of training. Access may be limited only if the business shows the animal poses a direct threat to health or safety, would cause substantial physical damage to property, or would substantially interfere with others' reasonable enjoyment.
maine.esa_note: An animal that provides only comfort or emotional support, without individual training to do work or tasks, is not a service animal under 5 M.R.S. 4553 and has no public-access rights in Maine. ESAs are, however, protected in housing as assistance animals under Maine's broader housing definition (see housing note).
maine.misrepresentation_penalty: Civil violation with a fine up to $1,000 for each occurrence under 17 M.R.S. 1314-A: knowingly misrepresenting an animal as a service animal or assistance animal, including creating or providing false documents, fitting a non-service animal with a harness, collar, vest, or sign, or falsely claiming the animal has completed training to perform disability-related tasks.
maine.housing_note: Under 5 M.R.S. 4582-A(3), a housing provider may not refuse an assistance animal or otherwise discriminate against a person with a disability who uses one, unless it shows the animal poses a direct threat to health or safety, would cause substantial physical damage to property, or would substantially interfere with others' reasonable enjoyment. The use of an assistance animal — which in housing includes an ESA determined necessary by a clinician — may not be conditioned on a fee or security deposit, though the tenant is liable for damage it causes.
maine.state_statute: Maine Human Rights Act, 5 M.R.S. 4553, 4582-A, 4592; White Cane Law, 17 M.R.S. 1311-1316, including 17 M.R.S. 1312 and 1314-A
maine.state_note: Maine's two-tier system is distinctive: a narrow dog-only service animal definition for public access, and a broader assistance animal definition for housing that covers ESAs. Maine also makes denying or interfering with a service animal's admittance a Class E crime under 17 M.R.S. 1314, carrying up to 6 months in jail and a fine up to $1,000 — one of the strongest access-denial penalties in the country. Note: the public-access definition is dog-only in the state text; miniature horses are covered federally under the ADA as a reasonable modification.
maine.sources: 5 M.R.S. 4553(9-E), 5 M.R.S. 4582-A(3), 5 M.R.S. 4592(8), 17 M.R.S. 1312, 17 M.R.S. 1314, 17 M.R.S. 1314-A, Maine Human Rights Commission, maine.gov/mhrc, legislature.maine.gov

maryland.service_animal_def: Under Human Services Article 7-701, a service animal is a guide dog, signal dog, or other animal individually trained to do work or perform tasks for a person with a disability. Maryland's definition says other animal rather than limiting it to dogs, so it is broader than the ADA on its face, though in practice public accommodations generally follow the ADA standard of dogs and, in limited cases, miniature horses. Service animal trainers are also covered.
maryland.public_access_note: Under Human Services Article 7-704, individuals with disabilities, parents of a minor child with a disability, and service animal trainers have the same right as others to full and free use of roads, sidewalks, public buildings, public facilities, and other public places, and full and equal access to common carriers, public conveyances, and places of public accommodation, including restaurants, stores, hotels, and government buildings, with no extra charge for the service animal, and are liable for damage it causes. A business may ask only the two ADA questions — whether the animal is required because of a disability and what work or task it performs — and may not demand documentation, certification, or a demonstration. A trainer may bring an animal being trained into a place of public accommodation except where it would create a clear danger of disturbance or physical harm (7-705(c)).
maryland.esa_note: Emotional support animals are not service animals under Maryland law or the ADA and have no public-access rights. In housing, however, an ESA may be a reasonable accommodation: the Maryland Commission on Civil Rights has issued guidance confirming that under the Maryland Fair Housing Act a reasonable accommodation may include an emotional support animal even when it has not been individually trained to perform a specific task.
maryland.misrepresentation_penalty: No specific state penalty for falsely claiming an animal is a service animal. Maryland is one of the few states with no fake-service-dog statute; it relies on general fraud and trespass provisions instead. Denying access to a person with a service animal, by contrast, is a misdemeanor with a fine up to $500 under Human Services Article 7-708.
maryland.housing_note: Under Human Services Article 7-704 and 7-705 and the Maryland Fair Housing Act, a housing provider must make a reasonable accommodation for a service animal or other assistance animal, including an emotional support animal, needed because of a disability, including waiving a no-pets rule, and may not charge a pet deposit or extra fee for the animal, though the tenant is liable for damage it causes. A provider may ask for reliable documentation of the disability-related need when it is not obvious. Maryland law was updated by SB 535 (2023), effective October 1, 2023, and also lets a handler keep a retired service dog in housing for life.
maryland.state_statute: Maryland Human Services Article, Title 7, Subtitle 7, sections 7-701 through 7-709 (Maryland Service Animal Reform Act, Gretchen's Law); Criminal Law Article 10-626 (harming a service animal)
maryland.state_note: Maryland is unusual in three ways: its service-animal definition says other animal rather than dogs only, it has an orange-tag licensing system for service dogs, and it has no misrepresentation penalty at all. Harming a service animal is a crime under Criminal Law 10-626, punishable by up to 2 years in prison.
maryland.sources: Md. Human Services 7-701, 7-704, 7-705, 7-708, Md. Criminal Law 10-626, Maryland Commission on Civil Rights ESA guidance, mccr.maryland.gov, mgaleg.maryland.gov

massachusetts.service_animal_def: Massachusetts has no standalone state definition in its public-access statute (M.G.L. c. 272, § 98A) and instead uses the ADA definition: a dog individually trained to do work or perform tasks for a person with a disability. Under the ADA, miniature horses may also qualify in limited circumstances. Service dogs in training are covered separately: under M.G.L. c. 129, § 39F, a person raising or training a service dog (including guide, hearing, or assistance dogs) has the same public-access rights as a person with a disability.
massachusetts.public_access_note: A person with a disability accompanied by a service dog has the same access as everyone else to public conveyances, amusements, restaurants, stores, hotels, and other places of public accommodation under M.G.L. c. 272, § 98A, with no extra charge. A business may ask only the two ADA questions: whether the dog is required because of a disability, and what work or task it has been trained to perform; it may not ask about the disability or demand documentation. Massachusetts goes beyond the ADA by giving service dogs in training full public-access rights and by requiring hearing dogs to wear a bright-colored collar and leash (M.G.L. c. 129, § 39C).
massachusetts.esa_note: Emotional support animals are not service animals under the ADA or Massachusetts law, so they have no right of access to restaurants, stores, hotels, or other public places. In housing, an emotional support animal may be allowed as a reasonable accommodation for a disability under state and federal fair housing law, with documentation, but that is a housing rule, not a public-access right.
massachusetts.misrepresentation_penalty: No specific state penalty. Massachusetts has no enacted law penalizing falsely claiming an animal is a service animal; bills to create one (for example, H.3657 in 2019 and H.1565 in 2021) passed the House but died in the Senate, and a later proposal would only create a study commission.
massachusetts.housing_note: Under M.G.L. c. 151B, § 4, housing providers must make reasonable accommodations for a person with a disability, including allowing a service animal in housing with a no-pets policy, and may not charge a pet deposit or extra fee for the service animal. A housing provider may ask for reliable documentation of the disability-related need when the need is not obvious.
massachusetts.state_statute: Massachusetts General Laws c. 272, § 98A (public access); c. 129, § 39F (service dogs in training); c. 151B, § 4 (housing and employment discrimination)
massachusetts.state_note: Massachusetts is unusually strong on service dogs in training, giving trainers the same access rights as handlers, and it allows treble damages for wrongful injury to an assistance animal under M.G.L. c. 272, § 85A. Denying access can bring a fine of up to $300 plus a civil forfeiture of at least $100 under § 98A.
massachusetts.sources: M.G.L. c. 272, § 98A; M.G.L. c. 129, §§ 39C, 39F; M.G.L. c. 151B, § 4; malegislature.gov bills H.3657 and H.1565; mass.gov MCAD pages

michigan.service_animal_def: Under MCL 750.502c, Michigan defines a service animal by reference to the federal rule at 28 CFR 36.104 — a dog individually trained to do work or perform tasks for a person with a disability — and adds an individually trained miniature horse that performs work or tasks for a person with a disability. The definition covers physical, sensory, psychiatric, intellectual, and other mental disabilities, and expressly includes veterans diagnosed with PTSD, traumatic brain injury, or another service-related disability. Service animals in training are also covered, accompanied by their raiser or trainer.
michigan.public_access_note: A person with a disability accompanied by a service animal must be allowed in places of public accommodation, including restaurants, stores, hotels, public transport, and government buildings, under MCL 750.502c, with no extra fee or surcharge and no requirement to show documentation. Staff may ask only the two ADA questions: whether the animal is required because of a disability, and what task it is trained to perform. Michigan also runs a voluntary service animal identification and patch program through the Michigan Department of Civil Rights (MCL 37.301-37.307), but registration is never required for access.
michigan.esa_note: Emotional support, therapy, and comfort animals are not service animals under Michigan law or the ADA, because their presence alone is not a trained task, so they have no public-access rights. In housing, an emotional support animal may be allowed as a reasonable accommodation under the Persons with Disabilities Civil Rights Act and the federal Fair Housing Act, with documentation when the need is not obvious.
michigan.misrepresentation_penalty: Misdemeanor under MCL 752.62 and 752.63: knowingly and falsely representing in a public place that you have a service animal or a service animal in training is punishable by up to 90 days in jail, a fine of up to $500, and/or up to 30 days of community service. Knowingly submitting a false affidavit for the state's voluntary service animal ID is a separate misdemeanor with the same penalty range (MCL 37.307).
michigan.housing_note: The Persons with Disabilities Civil Rights Act (MCL 37.1502) bars disability discrimination in housing, and a service animal must be allowed as a reasonable accommodation in housing with a no-pets policy, with no pet deposit or extra fee for the animal. A landlord may ask for documentation of the disability-related need when it is not obvious.
michigan.state_statute: Michigan Compiled Laws § 750.502c (service animals in public places); §§ 752.62-752.63 (misrepresentation); Persons with Disabilities Civil Rights Act, MCL 37.1101 et seq.
michigan.state_note: Michigan is one of the few states that writes miniature horses into its own service animal statute, and it is also one of the few with a state-run voluntary service animal identification program — but the ID is optional and a business may never demand it.
michigan.sources: MCL 750.502c; MCL 752.62-752.63; MCL 37.301-37.307; MCL 37.1502; michigan.gov MDCR service animals page

minnesota.service_animal_def: Minnesota defines 'service animal' by adopting the federal ADA definition (Minn. Stat. § 363A.19, subd. 3): a dog individually trained to do work or perform tasks for a person with a disability, with the work directly related to the disability. The statute does not list species itself, so the ADA rule controls — dogs, and miniature horses in limited circumstances under the ADA. A person training a dog to be a service dog has the same access rights under Minn. Stat. § 256C.02.
minnesota.public_access_note: It is an unfair discriminatory practice for the owner, operator, or manager of a hotel, restaurant, public conveyance, or other public place to bar a person with a disability accompanied by a service animal (Minn. Stat. § 363A.19), and no extra payment or charge may be required. A business may ask only the two ADA questions — whether the animal is required because of a disability, and what task it is trained to perform — and may not demand proof or documentation. A 2024 amendment (Laws 2024, c. 105) expanded the statute from only blind, deaf, and physical or sensory disabilities to all physical and mental disabilities, finally aligning state law with the ADA.
minnesota.esa_note: Emotional support animals are not service animals under Minnesota law or the ADA, so they have no right to enter restaurants, stores, hotels, or other public places. In housing, an assistance animal (including an emotional support animal) may be allowed as a reasonable accommodation under the Minnesota Human Rights Act and the federal Fair Housing Act, and a landlord may ask for documentation when the need is not obvious.
minnesota.misrepresentation_penalty: Under Minn. Stat. § 609.833, intentionally misrepresenting an animal as a service animal in a place of public accommodation is a petty misdemeanor on a first offense (maximum fine $300) and a misdemeanor on a second or subsequent offense (up to a $1,000 fine and/or up to 90 days in jail).
minnesota.housing_note: Under the Minnesota Human Rights Act (Minn. Stat. § 363A.09), a landlord must make reasonable accommodations for a person with a disability, including allowing a service animal or other assistance animal despite a no-pets policy, with no pet deposit or extra fee for the animal. Property owners who in good faith allow an assistance animal are also given immunity from liability for injury or damage caused by the animal (Minn. Stat. § 604A.302).
minnesota.state_statute: Minnesota Statutes § 363A.19 (public access); § 256C.02 (service dogs and trainers); § 609.833 (misrepresentation); Minnesota Human Rights Act, Minn. Stat. ch. 363A
minnesota.state_note: Minnesota's 2024 expansion of § 363A.19 to all physical and mental disabilities closed a long-standing gap that had left psychiatric service dog handlers relying on federal law alone. Minnesota also has one of the strongest tiered penalties in the country for harming a service animal (Minn. Stat. § 343.21).
minnesota.sources: Minn. Stat. §§ 363A.19, 256C.02, 609.833, 604A.302; Laws 2018, c. 106; Laws 2024, c. 105; revisor.mn.gov; mn.gov/mdhr

mississippi.service_animal_def: Under the Mississippi Support Animal Act, Miss. Code Ann. §§ 43-6-151 to 43-6-155, a 'support animal' is an animal individually trained to do work or perform tasks for the benefit of a person with a disability, including guide, seeing-eye, hearing-ear, and service animals.
