It is limited to a dog or miniature horse and does not include a pet. The Act also covers veterans diagnosed with PTSD. A person training a support animal has the same public-access rights as a person with a disability using one.
mississippi.public_access_note: Blind, mobility-impaired, and hearing-impaired persons (and veterans with PTSD) using a support animal are entitled to full and equal accommodations, advantages, facilities, and privileges of public conveyances, lodging places, and similar public places under Miss. Code Ann. § 43-6-155. A business may ask only the two ADA questions — whether the animal is required because of a disability, and what task it is trained to perform — and may not demand documentation or charge extra. Hearing dogs must wear a blaze orange leash or collar, a distinctive Mississippi identification rule.
mississippi.esa_note: Emotional support animals are not service animals under the ADA or the Mississippi Support Animal Act, so they have no right of access to public places. Mississippi has no state ESA statute and no state fair housing act, so housing rights for an emotional support animal rest entirely on the federal Fair Housing Act, with complaints going to HUD, not a state agency.
mississippi.misrepresentation_penalty: No specific state penalty. Mississippi has no statute criminalizing falsely claiming an animal is a service animal; the Support Animal Act contains only §§ 43-6-151, 43-6-153, and 43-6-155, and no misrepresentation section. (One secondary source cites a § 43-6-157 with a $500 fine, but that section does not appear in the Code's Support Animal Act.) Harassing or injuring a service animal is a separate misdemeanor under Miss. Code Ann. § 97-41-21, with up to 90 days in jail and/or a fine of up to $500.
mississippi.housing_note: Mississippi has no state fair housing act and no state fair-housing enforcement agency, so housing rights for service animals and assistance animals come from the federal Fair Housing Act: a landlord must allow a service animal or assistance animal as a reasonable accommodation despite a no-pets policy, with no pet deposit or fee, and may ask for documentation when the need is not obvious. Complaints go directly to HUD.
mississippi.state_statute: Mississippi Support Animal Act, Miss. Code Ann. §§ 43-6-151 to 43-6-155; Miss. Code Ann. § 97-41-21 (harming a service animal)
mississippi.agency_name: No state human rights agency in Mississippi — ADA complaints go to the U.S. Department of Justice
mississippi.state_note: Mississippi is one of the few states with no state human rights commission and no state fair housing law at all, so disability-access complaints in public places and housing must go to federal agencies (the U.S. Department of Justice for ADA access, HUD for housing). The blaze orange leash or collar requirement for hearing dogs is distinctive to Mississippi.
mississippi.sources: Miss. Code Ann. §§ 43-6-151, 43-6-153, 43-6-155, 97-41-21; law.justia.com Mississippi Code Title 43, ch. 6, art. 5; msbar.org free legal help listing

missouri.service_animal_def: Under RSMo § 209.200, a 'service dog' is a dog being or having been specially trained to do work or perform tasks that benefit a particular person with a disability, covering physical, sensory, psychiatric, intellectual, and other mental disabilities, including diabetes. The statute lists guide dogs, hearing dogs, medical alert or response dogs, mental health or psychiatric service dogs, mobility dogs, professional therapy dogs, and search and rescue dogs, including for persons with autism. Missouri's definition is dog-only at the state level; miniature horses are covered only through the ADA.
missouri.public_access_note: Every person with a disability has the right to be accompanied by a guide, hearing, or service dog in public places listed in RSMo § 209.150 — including restaurants, stores, hotels, public transport, and government buildings — without paying an extra charge, and the handler is liable only for damage the dog causes. A business may ask only the two ADA questions: whether the dog is required because of a disability, and what task it is trained to perform. Missouri's definition is broader than the ADA in one way: it expressly includes professional therapy dogs as service dogs.
missouri.esa_note: Emotional support animals are not service dogs under Missouri law or the ADA, because comfort or companionship alone is not a trained task, so they have no public-access rights. In housing, an assistance animal (including an emotional support animal) may be allowed as a reasonable accommodation under the Missouri Human Rights Act and the federal Fair Housing Act, with documentation when the need is not obvious.
missouri.misrepresentation_penalty: Class C misdemeanor under RSMo § 209.204 for knowingly impersonating a person with a disability to obtain service dog accommodations, or for misrepresenting a dog as a service dog — including using false documents, putting a vest or harness on a dog that is not a service dog, or claiming training that was not completed — plus civil liability for actual damages. A second or later violation is a class B misdemeanor. The same penalties apply to misrepresenting an animal as an assistance animal to get a Fair Housing Act accommodation.
missouri.housing_note: Under the Missouri Human Rights Act (RSMo § 213.040), a landlord may not discriminate in housing because of disability, and must allow a service dog or other assistance animal as a reasonable accommodation despite a no-pets policy, with no pet deposit or extra fee for the animal. A landlord may ask for documentation of the disability-related need when it is not obvious.
missouri.state_statute: Revised Statutes of Missouri §§ 209.150, 209.200, 209.204 (service animals); Missouri Human Rights Act, RSMo ch. 213
missouri.state_note: Missouri is unusual in two ways: its service dog definition expressly includes professional therapy dogs, and its misrepresentation law also reaches fake assistance-animal claims made to get housing accommodations, not just public-access claims. Complaints under the Missouri Human Rights Act must be filed with the MCHR within 180 days.
missouri.sources: RSMo §§ 209.150, 209.200, 209.204, 213.040; senate.mo.gov SB 225 summary; labor.mo.gov MCHR pages

montana.service_animal_def: Under Mont. Code Ann. § 49-4-203(2), a 'service animal' is a dog or miniature horse individually trained to provide assistance to an individual with a disability. The statute expressly states that the term does not include an emotional support animal. A person with a disability accompanied by a service animal in training also has access rights under § 49-4-214.
montana.public_access_note: A person with a disability has the right to be accompanied by a service animal or a service animal in training in any place listed in Mont. Code Ann. § 49-4-211(2), including restaurants, stores, hotels, public transport, and government buildings, without being charged extra for the animal, and the handler is liable for any damage the animal causes (§ 49-4-214). Staff may ask only the two ADA questions: whether the animal is required because of a disability, and what task it is trained to perform. Montana's law, revised by HB 439 in 2019, also lets a place of public accommodation file a complaint with local law enforcement if it suspects an animal is being misrepresented.
montana.esa_note: Emotional support animals are expressly excluded from Montana's service animal definition (§ 49-4-203(2)), so they have no public-access rights under state law or the ADA. In housing, an emotional support animal may still be allowed as a reasonable accommodation under the Montana Human Rights Act and the federal Fair Housing Act, with documentation when the need is not obvious.
montana.misrepresentation_penalty: Misdemeanor under Mont. Code Ann. §§ 49-4-221 and 49-4-222, but only after a written warning: a person is guilty only if they were previously given a written warning that it is illegal to intentionally misrepresent a service animal and then continued to do so. Fines are $50 for a first offense, $75 to $200 for a second offense, and $100 to $1,000 for a third or subsequent offense, and the court may also order community service for an organization that advocates for people with disabilities.
montana.housing_note: Under Mont. Code Ann. § 49-4-214(2), a person with a disability who has a service animal is entitled to full and equal access to all housing accommodations as provided in § 49-2-305, including allowing the animal despite a no-pets policy, with no pet deposit or extra fee. A landlord may ask for documentation of the disability-related need when it is not obvious.
montana.state_statute: Montana Code Annotated §§ 49-4-203, 49-4-211, 49-4-214, 49-4-221, 49-4-222; Montana Human Rights Act, MCA Title 49, ch. 2
montana.state_note: Montana's warning-first approach to misrepresentation is distinctive: a first-time offender who has never received a written warning cannot be criminally charged. The state also writes the emotional support animal exclusion directly into its service animal definition, and discrimination complaints must be filed with the Human Rights Bureau within 180 days.
montana.sources: MCA §§ 49-4-203, 49-4-214, 49-4-221, 49-4-222; 2019 HB 439; animallaw.info Montana assistance animal statutes; erd.dli.mt.gov Human Rights Bureau pages

nebraska.service_animal_def: Nebraska defines a service animal by reference to the ADA definition as it existed on January 1, 2008 (Neb. Rev. Stat. § 49-801(19)): a dog individually trained to do work or perform tasks for the benefit of a person with a disability, including a physical, sensory, psychiatric, intellectual, or other mental disability. The frozen 2008 reference means the state definition does not automatically update with federal changes. A bona fide trainer of a service animal has the same public-access rights while training (§ 20-127(3)).
nebraska.public_access_note: A totally or partially blind person, a deaf or hard-of-hearing person, or a physically disabled person has the right to be accompanied by a service animal in public places under Neb. Rev. Stat. § 20-127, including restaurants, stores, hotels, public transport, and government buildings, with no extra charge. A business may ask only the two ADA questions: whether the animal is required because of a disability, and what task it is trained to perform. Note the gap in state law: the public-access statutes name only blind, deaf, and physically disabled persons, so psychiatric service dog handlers rely on the federal ADA, which covers them fully and overrides the narrower state text.
nebraska.esa_note: Emotional support animals are not service animals under Nebraska law or the ADA, so they have no right to enter public places. In housing, an emotional support animal may be allowed as a reasonable accommodation under the Nebraska Fair Housing Act (Neb. Rev. Stat. §§ 20-301 et seq.) and the federal Fair Housing Act, with documentation when the need is not obvious.
nebraska.misrepresentation_penalty: No specific state penalty. Nebraska has no enacted law against misrepresenting an animal as a service animal: LB 491 (2017) would have made fraudulent misrepresentation a Class III misdemeanor for a first offense and a Class II misdemeanor for later offenses, but the bill was never enacted, and the current Neb. Rev. Stat. § 28-1009.01 covers only violence on or interference with a service animal (a Class III misdemeanor). Separately, unlawfully using a white cane or guide dog while not blind is a Class III misdemeanor under § 28-1313.
nebraska.housing_note: Under the Nebraska Fair Housing Act and Neb. Rev. Stat. §§ 20-131.01 to 20-131.04, a landlord must allow a service animal as a reasonable accommodation for a person with a disability despite a no-pets policy, and may not charge a pet deposit or extra fee for the animal. A landlord may ask for documentation of the disability-related need when it is not obvious.
nebraska.state_statute: Nebraska Revised Statutes §§ 20-126 to 20-131.04 (civil rights, service animals); § 49-801(19) (definition); § 28-1009.01 (violence on a service animal); Nebraska Fair Housing Act, §§ 20-301 et seq.
nebraska.state_note: Nebraska's state public-access law is narrower than the ADA — it names only blind, deaf, and physically disabled persons and freezes its service animal definition to the ADA as it stood on January 1, 2008 — so handlers with psychiatric service dogs should rely on federal ADA rights. Nebraska also has no misrepresentation penalty despite repeated bills, and service animals are licensed locally but no license tax may be charged (§ 54-603).
nebraska.sources: Neb. Rev. Stat. §§ 20-127, 28-1009.01, 28-1313, 49-801(19), 54-603; Nebraska Legislature LB 491 (2017) and Unicameral Update; nebraskalegislature.gov statute pages

nevada.service_animal_def: Under NRS 426.097, Nevada defines a service animal by reference to the federal definition at 28 CFR 36.104 — a dog individually trained to do work or perform tasks for a person with a disability — and expressly includes a miniature horse trained to do work or perform tasks. A service animal in training is a dog or miniature horse being trained as a service animal (NRS 426.099), and trainers have public-access rights too.
nevada.public_access_note: A person with a disability accompanied by a service animal or a service animal in training must be allowed in places of public accommodation (NRS 651.075), on public transportation (NRS 704.145 and 706.366), and in housing (NRS 118.105), including restaurants, stores, hotels, and government buildings, with no extra fee or deposit. A business may ask only the two ADA questions — whether the animal is required because of a disability, and what task it is trained to perform — and NRS 651.075 bars a business from requiring proof that the animal is a service animal. Nevada also makes refusing a service animal at work an unlawful employment practice (NRS 613.330).
nevada.esa_note: Emotional support animals are not service animals under Nevada law or the ADA, so they have no right to enter public places, and Nevada law makes it a misdemeanor to fraudulently misrepresent a pet or emotional support animal as a service animal. In housing, an emotional support animal may be allowed as a reasonable accommodation under the federal Fair Housing Act and Nevada fair housing law, with documentation when the need is not obvious.
nevada.misrepresentation_penalty: Misdemeanor under NRS 426.805: fraudulently misrepresenting an animal as a service animal or a service animal in training is punishable by a fine of not more than $500.
nevada.housing_note: Under NRS 118.105, a landlord may not refuse housing to a person with a disability because of a service animal, and may not charge an additional fee or deposit for the animal. A landlord may ask for documentation of the disability-related need when it is not obvious, and housing discrimination complaints go to the Nevada Equal Rights Commission.
nevada.state_note: Nevada has some of the most detailed service animal protections in the country: tiered criminal penalties for harming a service animal (interference is a gross misdemeanor; beating is a category E felony; killing is a category D felony under NRS 426.790), a $750 minimum floor for punitive damages against a business that denies access (NRS 426.820), and an explicit ban on employers refusing a service animal at work.
nevada.sources: NRS §§ 426.097, 426.099, 426.790, 426.805, 426.820, 651.075, 118.105, 613.330; leg.state.nv.us SB 36 (2005); detr.nv.gov NERC pages; nolo.com Nevada service animal laws

new hampshire.service_animal_def: Under RSA 167-D:1(IV), a 'service animal' is any dog individually trained to do work or perform tasks for the benefit of an individual with a disability, including a physical, sensory, psychiatric, intellectual, or other mental disability. Other species of animals, whether wild or domestic, trained or untrained, are not service animals under New Hampshire law — so miniature horses are not recognized at the state level (the ADA may still cover them). The work or task must be directly related to the handler's disability (RSA 167-D:2), and emotional support, comfort, or companionship alone does not count.
new hampshire.public_access_note: A service animal may accompany its handler or trainer into any public facility, housing accommodation, or place of public accommodation to which the general public is invited (RSA 167-D:4), including restaurants, stores, hotels, public transport, and government buildings, subject only to conditions that apply to everyone. A business may ask only the two ADA questions: whether the animal is required because of a disability, and what task it is trained to perform. New Hampshire goes beyond the ADA by giving service animal trainers the same access rights while training, and by having the Secretary of State provide businesses with a window decal stating service animals are welcome and misrepresentation violates RSA 167-D:8.
new hampshire.esa_note: Emotional support animals are not service animals under RSA chapter 167-D or the ADA — the statute says the provision of emotional support, well-being, comfort, or companionship does not constitute work or tasks — so they have no public-access rights. In housing, an emotional support animal may be allowed as a reasonable accommodation under RSA 354-A and the federal Fair Housing Act, with documentation when the need is not obvious.
new hampshire.misrepresentation_penalty: Misdemeanor under RSA 167-D:8 and 167-D:10. It is unlawful to impersonate a person with a disability to receive service dog accommodations, to fit an animal with a collar, vest, harness, sign, or tag representing it as a service animal when it is not, or to fraudulently request a service animal tag. Violations of the chapter are a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of up to $2,000 and up to 1 year in jail; some summaries describe the basic offense as a class B misdemeanor.
new hampshire.housing_note: Under RSA 167-D:4, a service animal may accompany its handler into any housing accommodation, and under RSA 354-A a housing provider must make reasonable accommodations for a person with a disability, including allowing a service animal despite a no-pets policy, with no pet deposit or extra fee. A landlord may ask for documentation of the disability-related need when it is not obvious.
new hampshire.state_statute: New Hampshire Revised Statutes Annotated ch. 167-D (Service Animals and Search and Rescue Dogs), §§ 167-D:1 to 167-D:10; RSA 354-A (Law Against Discrimination)
new hampshire.agency_name: New Hampshire Commission for Human Rights
new hampshire.state_note: New Hampshire's service animal definition is narrower than the ADA — dogs only, with no miniature horses at the state level — but its misrepresentation law is broader than most, reaching fake vests, harnesses, collars, and tags, not just spoken claims. The state also runs a service animal tag program, and the denial-of-access fine under the older White Cane Law (RSA 167-C:3) is only $25, a notably outdated amount.
new hampshire.sources: RSA ch. 167-D, §§ 167-D:1, 167-D:2, 167-D:4, 167-D:8, 167-D:10; RSA 354-A; gencourt.state.nh.us RSA 167-D pages; humanrights.nh.gov

new jersey.service_animal_def: Under the New Jersey Law Against Discrimination, N.J.S.A. 10:5-5(dd), a 'service dog' is any dog individually trained to the requirements of a person with a disability, including minimal protection work, rescue work, pulling a wheelchair, or retrieving dropped items, and it expressly includes a 'seizure dog' trained to alert or assist persons with epilepsy or other seizure disorders. A 'guide dog' is a dog trained to assist a person who is blind or deaf. The definition is dog-only at the state level; miniature horses are covered only through the ADA. A trainer actively engaged in training a service or guide dog has the same access rights (N.J.S.A. 10:5-29.3).
new jersey.public_access_note: A person with a disability accompanied by a service or guide dog is entitled to full and equal access to all public facilities under N.J.S.A. 10:5-29, including restaurants, stores, hotels, public transport, schools, and government buildings, with no extra charge. A business may ask only the two ADA questions: whether the dog is required because of a disability, and what task it is trained to perform, and may not demand documentation. New Jersey goes beyond the ADA with Charlie's Law (N.J.S.A. 10:5-29.11): escalating civil penalties for denying access — $250 for a first violation, $500 for a second, and $1,000 for a third and each later violation.
new jersey.esa_note: Emotional support animals are not service or guide dogs under New Jersey law or the ADA, so they have no right to enter public places. In housing, an emotional support, therapy, or assistance animal may be allowed as a reasonable accommodation under the Law Against Discrimination — it does not need to be specially trained, and other species can qualify — with documentation from a medical provider when the need is not obvious.
new jersey.misrepresentation_penalty: No general misrepresentation crime. New Jersey has no standalone statute criminalizing falsely claiming a pet is a service animal. The closest provision, N.J.S.A. 10:5-29.5, fines a person $100 to $500 for fitting a dog with a harness of the type commonly used by blind persons to represent it as a guide dog, or for intentionally interfering with a disabled person's rights or the dog's function; N.J.S.A. 10:5-29.10 sets a $100 to $500 fine for violating the act generally.
new jersey.housing_note: Under N.J.S.A. 10:5-29.2, a person with a disability who has a service or guide dog is entitled to full and equal access to all housing accommodations, with no extra charge for the dog, though the handler is liable for any damage the dog causes. Uniquely, a person with a disability may keep a retired service or guide dog in housing after it retires from active service. Emotional support animals are also covered in housing as reasonable accommodations under the Law Against Discrimination.
new jersey.agency_name: New Jersey Division on Civil Rights (DCR)
new jersey.state_note: New Jersey's protections are among the strongest in the country: its service dog definition is broader than the ADA (it includes minimal protection work and seizure dogs by name), Charlie's Law sets escalating civil penalties for denying access, and retired service dogs keep their housing protection. Complaints to the Division on Civil Rights must be filed within 180 days.
new jersey.sources: N.J.S.A. 10:5-5(dd), 10:5-29, 10:5-29.2, 10:5-29.3, 10:5-29.5, 10:5-29.10, 10:5-29.11; njoag.gov Division on Civil Rights pages; nj.gov DCR guidance on assistance animals in housing

new mexico.service_animal_def: A 'qualified service animal' is a qualified service dog or a qualified service miniature horse that has been or is being trained to work or perform tasks for the benefit of a person with a disability, including guide dogs, hearing dogs, and service dogs. It does not include a pet, an emotional support animal, a comfort animal, or a therapy animal. (NMSA 1978, Section 28-11-2)
new mexico.public_access_note: A qualified service animal must be admitted to any building open to the public, all public accommodations such as restaurants, hotels, hospitals, swimming pools, stores, and theaters, and all common carriers, while under the control of the person with a disability or a trainer. No extra charge may be made for the animal, though the handler is liable for any damage it causes. Under the ADA, a business may ask only two questions when it is not obvious: whether the animal is required because of a disability, and what work or task it has been trained to perform; it may not ask about the disability or demand certification. New Mexico goes beyond the ADA by expressly covering animals still in training.
new mexico.esa_note: Emotional support, comfort, and therapy animals are expressly excluded from New Mexico's definition of a qualified service animal, so they have no public-access rights in the state. They may still qualify as assistance animals in housing as a reasonable accommodation under federal and state fair housing law.
new mexico.misrepresentation_penalty: Misdemeanor under NMSA 1978, Section 28-11-6: it is unlawful to knowingly present as a qualified service animal any animal that does not meet the Section 28-11-2 definition, punishable under Section 31-19-1 NMSA 1978. The Governor's Commission on Disability describes the penalty as a fine of up to $1,000 and/or jail time.
new mexico.housing_note: A person with a disability may keep a qualified service animal in housing as a reasonable accommodation, with no extra charge or pet deposit for the animal, though the handler is liable for damage it causes. A landlord may ask for documentation of the disability-related need only if the disability or need is not readily apparent.
new mexico.state_statute: New Mexico Service Animal Act, NMSA 1978, Sections 28-11-1 to 28-11-6; also the White Cane Law, NMSA 1978, Sections 28-7-1 to 28-7-7
new mexico.agency_name: New Mexico Department of Workforce Solutions, Human Rights Bureau
new mexico.state_note: New Mexico's law is broader than the ADA in two ways: it expressly covers service animals in training, and its White Cane Law separately guarantees guide-dog access for people who are blind. The Service Animal Act was renamed from the Assistance Animal Act in 2013, when the misrepresentation penalty was added.
new mexico.sources: NMSA 1978 Sections 28-11-2, 28-11-3, 28-11-6 (nmlegis.gov, Justia), Nolo New Mexico service dog laws, New Mexico Department of Workforce Solutions Human Rights Bureau

new york.service_animal_def: New York law covers guide dogs, hearing dogs, and service dogs. Civil Rights Law Section 47-b defines a service dog by reference to the federal ADA regulations: a dog under the control of the person using or training it that has been or is being individually trained to do work or perform tasks for a person with a disability, including psychiatric disabilities. The state statute speaks only of dogs; it does not include miniature horses in its own definition.
new york.public_access_note: No person may be denied admittance to or equal use of any public facility because they are accompanied by a guide, hearing, or service dog, including restaurants, stores, hotels, theaters, schools, government buildings, and all public and private transportation and housing accommodations. No extra charge or security deposit may be imposed for the dog, though the handler is liable for damage. Under the ADA, staff may ask only two questions when it is not obvious: whether the dog is a service animal required because of a disability, and what work or task it has been trained to perform. New York goes beyond the ADA by expressly counting all forms of public and private housing as public facilities.
new york.esa_note: Emotional support animals are not service animals under either New York law or the ADA, because they provide companionship rather than trained tasks, so they have no right to enter stores, restaurants, or other public places. They may still be protected in housing as a reasonable accommodation under the New York Human Rights Law and federal fair housing law.
new york.misrepresentation_penalty: New York has no general criminal penalty for falsely claiming a pet is a service animal. The enacted law, Agriculture and Markets Law Section 118 (effective December 18, 2017), makes it unlawful to knowingly apply a false or improper identification tag designating a dog as a guide, service, therapy, or hearing dog, punishable by a fine of up to $100 and up to 15 days in jail. A proposed Penal Law Section 242.20 offense carrying a $250 fine was introduced as a bill only and was not enacted.
new york.housing_note: Civil Rights Law Section 47 treats all forms of public and private housing accommodations as public facilities, so a person with a disability may keep a guide, hearing, or service dog in housing with no extra charge or security deposit, while remaining liable for damage. An emotional support animal may also be allowed in housing as a reasonable accommodation, with documentation if the need is not apparent.
new york.state_statute: New York Civil Rights Law, Article 4-B, Sections 47 to 47-c; New York Executive Law Section 296(14); Agriculture and Markets Law Section 118
new york.agency_name: New York State Division of Human Rights
new york.state_note: New York expressly gives trainers the same public-access rights as handlers while training a dog (Civil Rights Law Section 47-b(3)), and denying access is an unlawful discriminatory practice under Executive Law Section 296(14). Repeat violations of Sections 47 or 47-b within two years can bring a $1,000 fine under Section 47-c. New York City's Human Rights Law adds further local protections.
new york.sources: NY Civil Rights Law Sections 47, 47-b, 47-c (nysenate.gov), NY Executive Law Section 296(14), Agriculture and Markets Law Section 118, Nolo New York service dog laws, NY Division of Human Rights

north carolina.service_animal_def: North Carolina has no separate statutory definition of a service animal. General Statute Section 168-4.2 describes it as an animal trained to assist a person with his or her specific disability, without limiting it to dogs in the state text. In practice the federal ADA definition is used: a dog individually trained to do work or perform tasks directly related to the person's disability, with miniature horses allowed in some cases under the ADA.
north carolina.public_access_note: Every person with a disability has the right to be accompanied by a service animal in any place listed in General Statute Section 168-3, including public accommodations, common carriers, hotels, restaurants, and other places the public is invited, and to keep the animal on any premises the person leases, rents, or uses. No extra compensation, fee, or deposit may be charged for the animal. Under the ADA, a business may ask only two questions when it is not obvious: whether the animal is required because of a disability, and what work or task it has been trained to perform; it may not ask about the disability or demand proof. North Carolina's distinctive feature is a free, voluntary, permanent service animal registration tag issued by the Department of Health and Human Services, which is one way to show eligibility but is not required.
north carolina.esa_note: Emotional support animals are not service animals under the ADA or North Carolina law, so they have no public-access rights in the state. They may still qualify as assistance animals in housing as a reasonable accommodation under the North Carolina Fair Housing Act and federal fair housing law.
north carolina.misrepresentation_penalty: Class 3 misdemeanor under N.C. Gen. Stat. Section 168-4.5: it is unlawful to disguise an animal as a service animal or service animal in training. The statute sets the classification; secondary sources report a fine of up to $200 and up to 20 days in jail for a Class 3 misdemeanor of this type.
north carolina.housing_note: A person with a disability has the right to keep a service animal on any premises the person leases, rents, or uses, with no extra fee or deposit for the animal (N.C. Gen. Stat. Sections 168-4.2 and 168-4.4). A landlord may ask for documentation of the disability-related need for an assistance animal, including an emotional support animal, if the disability or need is not readily apparent.
north carolina.state_statute: North Carolina General Statutes, Chapter 168, Article 1, Sections 168-4.2 to 168-4.5 (Persons with Disabilities — Rights)
north carolina.agency_name: North Carolina Human Relations Commission, Civil Rights Division, Office of Administrative Hearings
north carolina.state_note: North Carolina expressly covers animals in training: an animal in training may enter public places when accompanied by its trainer and wearing a collar and leash, harness, or cape identifying it as a service animal in training, with the trainer liable for any damage (Section 168-4.2(b)). The state also operates a free, permanent, voluntary service animal registration tag program through the Department of Health and Human Services (Section 168-4.3).
north carolina.sources: N.C. Gen. Stat. Sections 168-4.2, 168-4.3, 168-4.4, 168-4.5 (ncleg.gov), Nolo penalties for faking a service dog, NC Office of Administrative Hearings Civil Rights Division

north dakota.service_animal_def: A service animal is any dog or miniature horse trained to do work, perform tasks, or provide assistance for the benefit of an individual with a disability, including pulling a wheelchair, lending balance support, retrieving dropped objects, or providing assistance in a medical crisis. The miniature horse provision was added by HB 1230 in 2021, bringing the statute into line with the ADA. (N.D. Cent. Code Section 25-13-01.1)
north dakota.public_access_note: A person with a disability is entitled to be accompanied by a service animal in places of public accommodation, common carriers, health care provider facilities, and all places to which the public is generally invited, with no extra charge for the animal, though the handler is liable for damage to the premises. Under the ADA, a business may ask only two questions when it is not obvious: whether the animal is required because of a disability, and what work or task it has been trained to perform. North Dakota goes beyond the ADA by making it a Class A misdemeanor to deny or interfere with admission or enjoyment of those places (Section 25-13-04).
north dakota.esa_note: Emotional support animals are not service animals under North Dakota law or the ADA, because their sole function is comfort or emotional support rather than trained tasks, so they have no public-access rights. They may still qualify as assistance animals in housing as a reasonable accommodation under state and federal fair housing law.
north dakota.misrepresentation_penalty: Infraction under N.D. Cent. Code Section 25-13-02.2: a person is guilty of an infraction if, in an attempt to gain admission to a public place or obtain a reasonable housing accommodation under Section 47-16-07.5, the person knowingly makes a false claim that a pet is a service animal. Sources disagree on the dollar amount: the 2019 bill text set a maximum fine of $100, while other sources report the general infraction maximum of $1,000; the text of Section 25-13-02.2 itself states no dollar amount.
north dakota.housing_note: A service animal must be allowed in housing as a reasonable accommodation under N.D. Cent. Code Section 47-16-07.5, with no pet deposit or extra fee for the animal. A landlord may ask for documentation if the disability or need is not apparent, and knowingly providing fraudulent disability documentation for a housing accommodation can lead to eviction and a damage fee of up to $1,000 under Section 47-16-07.6.
north dakota.state_statute: North Dakota Century Code, Chapter 25-13 (Blind and Disabled Persons' Activities), Sections 25-13-01.1 to 25-13-06; N.D. Cent. Code Section 47-16-07.5 (housing)
north dakota.agency_name: North Dakota Department of Labor and Human Rights, Human Rights Division
north dakota.state_note: Trainers have express public-access rights: a trainer with a service animal in training may enter public places if the trainer notifies the onsite manager, wears a photo ID issued by a nationally recognized service animal training program, and accepts financial responsibility for damage (Section 25-13-02.1). Denying access to a service animal team is a Class A misdemeanor, a stronger penalty than in most states.
north dakota.sources: N.D. Cent. Code Chapter 25-13, Sections 25-13-01.1, 25-13-02, 25-13-02.1, 25-13-02.2, 25-13-04 (ndlegis.gov, Justia), HB 1230 (2021) and HB 1259 (2019) bill texts, ND Department of Labor and Human Rights

ohio.service_animal_def: Ohio uses the term 'assistance dog': a dog trained by a nonprofit or for-profit special agency as a guide dog (for a blind person), a hearing dog (for a deaf or hearing-impaired person), or a service dog (for a person with a mobility impairment), including dogs still in training. A broader term, 'animal assistant,' is used in public-accommodation and housing rules and means any animal which aids a person with a disability. (Ohio Rev. Code Sections 955.011 and 955.43; Ohio Admin. Code 4112-5-02)
ohio.public_access_note: A person who is blind, deaf, hearing impaired, or has a mobility impairment, or a trainer of an assistance dog, is entitled to full and equal access to all public conveyances, hotels, lodging places, places of public accommodation, amusement, or resort, institutions of education, and other places the general public is invited, and may take the dog into those places. No fee or charge may be made for the dog, though the dog may not occupy a seat on a public conveyance and must be leashed on a common carrier. Under the ADA, a business may ask only two questions when it is not obvious: whether the animal is required because of a disability, and what work or task it has been trained to perform. Ohio's broader 'animal assistant' definition can cover animals beyond dogs in public-accommodation and housing contexts.
ohio.esa_note: Emotional support animals are not assistance dogs under Ohio Rev. Code Chapter 955 and have no public-access rights as service animals. They may still qualify as an 'animal assistant' or assistance animal in housing as a reasonable accommodation under Ohio and federal fair housing law.
ohio.misrepresentation_penalty: No specific state penalty for falsely claiming an animal is a service animal. Ohio has no targeted fake service dog or misrepresentation statute; general fraud laws could theoretically apply, but there is no specific service-animal misrepresentation offense. By contrast, recklessly denying access to or charging a fee for an assistance dog is a misdemeanor of the fourth degree under Ohio Rev. Code Section 955.43, punishable by up to 30 days in jail and a fine of up to $250.
ohio.housing_note: An assistance animal or animal assistant must be allowed in housing as a reasonable accommodation, with no pet deposit or extra fee for the animal, though the handler is liable for damage. A landlord may ask for documentation of the disability-related need only if the disability or need is not readily apparent.
ohio.state_statute: Ohio Revised Code Sections 955.011, 955.43, and 955.99; Ohio Revised Code Chapter 4112 (Ohio Civil Rights Act); Ohio Admin. Code 4112-5-02
ohio.state_note: Ohio's definition of a person with a mobility impairment was significantly expanded by HB 33, effective October 3, 2023. Ohio also designates the last week of July as Service Dog Awareness Week, and killing an assistance dog is a third-degree felony under Ohio Rev. Code Section 2921.321.
ohio.sources: Ohio Rev. Code Sections 955.011, 955.43 (codes.ohio.gov), Disability Rights Ohio service animals fact sheet, Ohio Civil Rights Commission

oklahoma.service_animal_def: Under Title 4, Section 801, as amended by HB 1178 effective November 1, 2025, a service animal is a dog individually trained to do work or perform tasks for the benefit of an individual with a disability, matching the ADA definition, and it does not include an emotional support animal or a therapy animal. The older Title 7, Section 19.1 law is narrower: a guide dog, signal dog, or service dog, with 'service dog' defined only for a physically handicapped person, and a signal dog must wear an orange identifying collar.
oklahoma.public_access_note: A person with a disability accompanied by a guide, signal, or service dog may not be denied admittance to streets, sidewalks, common carriers, hotels, motels, lodging, public buildings, educational facilities, restaurants, or any other place of public accommodation, amusement, convenience, or resort, with no extra charge for the dog, though the handler is liable for damage. Trainers from a recognized training center have the same access while training. Under the ADA, a business may ask only two questions when it is not obvious: whether the animal is required because of a disability, and what work or task it has been trained to perform. Oklahoma is distinctive in requiring businesses to post signage about service animal rights and in requiring an orange collar for signal dogs.
oklahoma.esa_note: Emotional support animals and therapy animals are expressly excluded from the definition of a service animal under Title 4, Section 801, so they have no public-access rights in Oklahoma. They may still qualify as assistance animals in housing as a reasonable accommodation under Oklahoma and federal fair housing law.
oklahoma.misrepresentation_penalty: Misdemeanor under 4 Okla. Stat. Section 801(E) and (F), as amended by HB 1178 effective November 1, 2025: knowingly presenting any animal or therapy animal as a service animal, or intentionally misrepresenting entitlement to an animal as a qualified service animal to obtain disability rights or benefits, is a misdemeanor upon conviction. The statute sets no dollar fine amount in that section. Denying access under Title 7, Section 19.2 is also a misdemeanor.
oklahoma.housing_note: A service dog must be allowed in housing as a reasonable accommodation under 41 Okla. Stat. Section 113.1, with no extra charge or pet deposit for the animal. A landlord may ask for documentation of the disability-related need if it is not readily apparent, and a knowingly false disability claim or fraudulent documentation to obtain a housing accommodation can lead to eviction remedies and damages of up to $1,000 under Section 113.2.
oklahoma.state_statute: Oklahoma Statutes, Title 4, Section 801 (Public Accommodations and Service Animals, as amended by HB 1178, 2025); Title 7, Sections 19.1 to 19.2; Title 41, Section 113.1 (housing)
oklahoma.agency_name: Oklahoma Attorney General, Office of Civil Rights Enforcement (successor to the Oklahoma Human Rights Commission)
oklahoma.state_note: HB 1178, enacted in 2025 by legislative veto override and effective November 1, 2025, aligned Oklahoma's definition with the ADA, added the misrepresentation misdemeanors, and requires public accommodations to post signage about service animal rights. Oklahoma's employment anti-discrimination law applies to employers with just one or more employees.
oklahoma.sources: 4 Okla. Stat. Section 801 (2025) (Justia, oklegislature.gov HB 1178), 7 Okla. Stat. Section 19.1 (Justia), Oklahoma House HB 1178 news release, Oklahoma Attorney General Office of Civil Rights Enforcement

oregon.service_animal_def: Oregon uses the term 'assistance animal': a dog or other animal designated by administrative rule that has been individually trained to do work or perform tasks for the benefit of an individual with a disability. Oregon Administrative Rule 839-006-0345 designates dogs and miniature horses as assistance animals. An 'assistance animal trainee' is an animal undergoing training to do work or tasks directly related to the person's disability. (ORS 659A.143)
oregon.public_access_note: A place of public accommodation or of access to state government services, programs, or activities may not deny a person with a disability or an assistance animal trainer the right to be accompanied by an assistance animal or trainee in any area open to the public or business invitees, including restaurants, stores, hotels, public transport, and government buildings. No fee or admission charge may be imposed for the animal, and no documentation may be required. A business may ask only two questions when it is not obvious: whether the animal is required due to a disability, and what work or task it is trained or being trained to perform; it may not ask about the nature or extent of the disability. Oregon goes beyond the ADA by expressly covering trainees and by barring any documentation demand in the statute itself.
oregon.esa_note: Emotional support, therapy, comfort, and companion animals are not assistance animals under Oregon law or the ADA, because they are not individually trained to do work or tasks, so they have no public-access rights. They may still qualify as assistance animals in housing as a reasonable accommodation under Oregon and federal fair housing law, where the definition is broader.
oregon.misrepresentation_penalty: No specific state penalty for falsely claiming an animal is a service animal. Oregon has no targeted fake service dog or misrepresentation statute; bills in 2019 (HB 2758 and HB 3098) failed to pass. Interfering with an assistance animal is a separate offense, a Class A misdemeanor under ORS 167.352, punishable by up to 364 days in jail and a fine of up to $6,250.
oregon.housing_note: An assistance animal must be allowed in housing as a reasonable accommodation under ORS 659A.145, with no pet deposit or extra fee for the animal, though the handler is liable for damage it causes. A landlord may ask for documentation of the disability-related need only if the disability or need is not readily apparent, and in housing the term can include emotional support animals that qualify as a reasonable accommodation.
oregon.state_statute: Oregon Revised Statutes Section 659A.143 (Assistance animals); ORS 659A.139, 659A.141, 659A.145; Oregon Admin. Rule 839-006-0345
oregon.agency_name: Oregon Bureau of Labor and Industries, Civil Rights Division
oregon.state_note: Oregon's disability definition carries an express 'construe broadly' mandate (ORS 659A.139), directing courts and agencies to interpret disability protections more expansively than the ADA. Oregon also exempts assistance animal owners from dog license fees (ORS 609.105) and allows civil penalties of up to $50,000 for a first discrimination violation and up to $100,000 for later violations.
oregon.sources: ORS 659A.143 (Justia, 2025), Northwest ADA Center service animals comparison guide, Oregon Bureau of Labor and Industries Civil Rights Division

pennsylvania.service_animal_def: A 'service, guide or support dog' is a dog that is trained or is being trained to work or perform tasks for the benefit of an individual with a disability, consistent with federal and state law related to service animals. The Pennsylvania Human Relations Commission uses a similar definition covering a dog or miniature horse individually trained to do work or tasks for a person with a disability. (18 Pa.C.S. Sections 5531 and 7325)
pennsylvania.public_access_note: It is a summary offense for the proprietor, manager, or employee of a theater, hotel, restaurant, or other place of public accommodation to refuse access to a person using a service, guide, or support dog or other aid animal, including trainers of such dogs. Service animals must be allowed in restaurants, retail stores, hotels, theaters, hospitals, professional offices, and public transportation, in all areas customers are normally allowed. Under the ADA, staff may ask only two questions when it is not obvious: whether the dog is a service animal required because of a disability, and what work or task it has been trained to perform; no certification or license is required. The Pennsylvania Human Relations Act also makes denial an unlawful discriminatory practice.
pennsylvania.esa_note: Emotional support animals are not service animals, because they are not trained to perform a specific task, so they cannot be taken into stores, restaurants, or other public accommodations as service dogs. They are, however, protected in housing as assistance animals that qualify as a reasonable accommodation under the Pennsylvania Human Relations Act and federal fair housing law.
pennsylvania.misrepresentation_penalty: Pennsylvania's misrepresentation penalties apply to housing only, under the Assistance and Service Animal Integrity Act, Act 118 of 2018 (68 P.S. Sections 405.5 to 405.6). Misrepresenting a disability or disability-related need for an assistance or service animal in housing, or making materially false statements to obtain documentation, is a misdemeanor of the third degree, punishable by up to one year in prison and a fine of up to $2,500. Misrepresenting an animal as an assistance or service animal in housing, including with a false document or by fitting it with a harness, collar, vest, or sign, is a summary offense with a fine of up to $1,000. There is no general public-access misrepresentation offense.
pennsylvania.housing_note: A service or assistance animal, including an emotional support animal that qualifies as a reasonable accommodation, must be allowed in housing with no pet deposit or extra fee, though the handler is liable for damage. Under the Assistance and Service Animal Integrity Act (68 P.S. Section 405.3), a landlord may request documentation of the disability and disability-related need only if the disability or need is not readily apparent or known to the landlord.
pennsylvania.state_statute: Pennsylvania Human Relations Act, 43 P.S. Sections 951 to 963; 18 Pa.C.S. Section 7325 (discrimination on account of guide, signal or service dog); Assistance and Service Animal Integrity Act, Act 118 of 2018, 68 P.S. Sections 405.1 to 405.7
pennsylvania.state_note: Pennsylvania is distinctive in targeting its fraud penalties at housing rather than public places, and in giving the Human Relations Commission detailed guidance distinguishing service animals, assistance animals, and emotional support animals across housing, public accommodations, education, and employment. Trainers of service, guide, or support dogs have the same public-access rights as handlers under 18 Pa.C.S. Section 7325.
pennsylvania.sources: 18 Pa.C.S. Sections 5531, 7325 (legis.state.pa.us), 68 P.S. Sections 405.1 to 405.7, Act 118 of 2018, Pennsylvania Human Relations Commission assistance animal guidance (pa.gov), Nolo Pennsylvania service dog laws

rhode island.service_animal_def: A service animal is a dog that has been, or is being, specifically trained to assist an individual with a disability, including a guide dog specially trained to aid a person who is blind or visually impaired, a hearing dog specially trained to aid a person who is deaf or hard of hearing, and a service dog specially trained to aid a person with another type of disability. The state definition covers dogs only; miniature horses are covered only through the ADA. (R.I. Gen. Laws Section 40-9.1-1.1)
rhode island.public_access_note: Every person with a disability may be accompanied by a service animal in any place listed in R.I. Gen. Laws Section 40-9.1-1, including public streets, buildings, transportation, schools, hotels, restaurants, theaters, and all other places to which the general public is invited, with no extra charge for the animal, though the handler is solely liable for damage it causes. Under the ADA, a business may ask only two questions when it is not obvious: whether the animal is required because of a disability, and what work or task it has been trained to perform; it may not ask about the disability or demand certification. Rhode Island also expressly covers trainers and puppy raisers of service animals.
rhode island.esa_note: Emotional support animals are not service animals under Rhode Island law or the ADA, so they have no public-access rights. They are, however, expressly protected in housing: state regulations cover the presence or desired presence of a personal assistive animal or emotional support animal for a person with disabilities in housing.
rhode island.misrepresentation_penalty: Civil violation under R.I. Gen. Laws Section 40-9.1-3.1: it is a violation to expressly represent that a pet or other animal is a service animal to gain access to a public area, when the person knew or should have known the animal did not meet the definition. The penalty is up to 30 hours of community service for an organization serving people with disabilities. There is no fine in the enacted text; a proposed $500 fine appeared in the bill only and was not enacted.
rhode island.housing_note: A person with a disability who has a guide dog or other personal assistive animal has full and equal access to covered housing, with no extra charge for the animal (R.I. Gen. Laws Sections 40-9.1-1(c), 40-9.1-2, and 34-37-4(e)). An emotional support animal may also be allowed in housing as a reasonable accommodation, with documentation if the disability or need is not apparent.
rhode island.state_statute: Rhode Island General Laws, Chapter 40-9.1 (Equal Rights of Blind and Deaf Persons to Public Facilities), Sections 40-9.1-1 to 40-9.1-5; R.I. Gen. Laws Section 34-37-4(e) (housing)
rhode island.agency_name: Rhode Island Commission for Human Rights
rhode island.state_note: Rhode Island's misrepresentation law, added in 2019, is unusual in using community service rather than a fine, and it directs the Commission for Human Rights to provide businesses with a decal stating that service animals are welcome and that misrepresentation is a violation of Rhode Island law. Trainers and puppy raisers have the same access rights as handlers under Section 40-9.1-2.1.
rhode island.sources: R.I. Gen. Laws Sections 40-9.1-1, 40-9.1-1.1, 40-9.1-2, 40-9.1-2.1, 40-9.1-3.1 (rilegislature.gov), Nolo Rhode Island service dog laws, Rhode Island Commission for Human Rights

south carolina.service_animal_def: A service animal or service animal-in-training is an animal trained or being trained to do work or perform tasks for an individual with a disability, including a physical, sensory, psychiatric, intellectual, or other mental disability. The definition is limited to a dog or a miniature horse, and emotional support, comfort, or companionship does not count as work or tasks. No vest, marking, or documentation is required for an animal to qualify. (S.C. Code Section 47-3-920)
south carolina.public_access_note: A person with a disability has the same right as anyone else to full and free use of public places and full and equal accommodations, including common carriers, hotels, lodging, restaurants, retail establishments, and places of public accommodation, amusement, or resort, accompanied by an assistance dog with no extra charge, though the handler is liable for damage. Trainers of assistance or guide dogs have the same access while engaged in training. Under the ADA, a business may ask only two questions when it is not obvious: whether the animal is required because of a disability, and what work or task it has been trained to perform. South Carolina's Layla's Law lets places of public accommodation set their own rules for non-service animals, including emotional support animals (Section 47-3-990).
south carolina.esa_note: Emotional support animals are not service animals under South Carolina law or the ADA, because emotional support, comfort, or companionship does not count as work or tasks, so they have no public-access rights, and businesses may set their own rules for them. They may still qualify as assistance animals in housing as a reasonable accommodation under South Carolina and federal fair housing law.
south carolina.misrepresentation_penalty: Civil fine, not a criminal offense, under S.C. Code Section 47-3-980 (2019 Act No. 44): intentionally misrepresenting an animal as a service animal or service animal-in-training to obtain a right or privilege provided to a disabled person is unlawful, with a fine of up to $250 for a first offense, up to $500 for a second offense, and up to $1,000 for a third or later offense. No custodial arrest may be made except on a warrant for failure to appear or failure to pay the fine. Earlier bill drafts had proposed misdemeanor fines of $350 to $5,000, but the enacted law uses the lower civil fines above.
south carolina.housing_note: A person with a disability who has an assistance dog has full and equal access to covered housing, with no extra charge for the animal (S.C. Code Section 43-33-70(d)). Under Section 31-21-70, added by 2019 Act No. 44, a landlord may ask certain questions about a tenant's or prospective tenant's animal for a reasonable accommodation, following a codified two-question process; no pet deposit or fee may be charged for an assistance animal.
south carolina.state_statute: South Carolina Code, Title 47, Chapter 3, Article 15, Layla's Law, Sections 47-3-910 to 47-3-990; S.C. Code, Title 43, Chapter 33, Sections 43-33-20, 43-33-40, and 43-33-70
south carolina.state_note: South Carolina is unusually strict toward businesses that deny access: interfering with a person's service-animal access rights is a misdemeanor under Section 43-33-40, and the state guide reports penalties of up to 3 years imprisonment for denying access. The state also designates October 15 as White Cane Safety Day, and its service-animal rules are split between two parts of the code, the older Title 43 access law and the newer Title 47 Layla's Law.
south carolina.sources: S.C. Code Sections 47-3-920, 47-3-980, 47-3-990 (scstatehouse.gov, Justia), S.C. Code Sections 43-33-20, 43-33-40, 43-33-70, 2019 Act No. 44 (S.281), South Carolina Human Affairs Commission

south dakota.service_animal_def: South Dakota's public-access law (SDCL 20-13-23.2) covers a person who is totally or partially physically disabled, blind, deaf, or has a psychiatric or mental disability, accompanied by a specially trained service animal, without limiting the term to dogs in that section. The misrepresentation law (SDCL 22-35-9) defines a service animal more narrowly as a dog trained to do work or perform tasks directly related to the person's disability; crime-deterrent effects and emotional support, well-being, comfort, or companionship do not count as work or tasks. A service animal in training is a dog that has completed basic obedience training and is housebroken (SDCL 20-13-1(17)), and its trainer must be affiliated with a nationally recognized training program.
south dakota.public_access_note: A person with a disability may be accompanied by a specially trained service animal in hotels, lodging, public accommodations, amusement or resort places, and other places open to the public (SDCL 20-13-23.1 and 20-13-23.2), with no extra charge, though the handler is liable for damage the animal causes. A business may ask only the two ADA questions when the need is not obvious: whether the animal is required because of a disability, and what work or task it has been trained to perform; it may not demand certification or proof of training. Denying access is a Class 2 misdemeanor, and service animals in training have public access if they wear a collar and leash, harness, or cape identifying them as in training.
south dakota.esa_note: Emotional support animals are not service animals under the ADA and have no public-access rights in South Dakota. In housing, however, SDCL 43-32-33 defines 'service animal' broadly to include emotional support animals, therapy animals, and assistance animals.
south dakota.misrepresentation_penalty: Class 2 misdemeanor under SDCL 22-35-9, enacted by 2026 Senate Bill 82 (signed March 9, 2026, effective July 1, 2026) — intentionally misrepresenting an animal as a service animal in a place of public accommodation to obtain rights the person knows they are not entitled to. A Class 2 misdemeanor carries up to 30 days in jail and/or a fine of up to $500.
south dakota.housing_note: A landlord may not prohibit by lease or otherwise the keeping of a service animal in a rented or leased residence (SDCL 20-13-23.4, violation a Class 2 misdemeanor), and no extra charge may be imposed for the animal. Under SDCL 43-32-33 through 43-32-36, a landlord may require reliable supporting documentation from a licensed health care provider confirming the disability and the disability-related need, unless the need is readily apparent or already known, and may not accept documentation from a provider who operates in the state solely to provide service or assistance animal certifications.
south dakota.state_statute: South Dakota Human Relations Act, SDCL Chapter 20-13, especially SDCL 20-13-23.1, 20-13-23.2, and 20-13-23.4; misrepresentation at SDCL 22-35-9; housing documentation at SDCL 43-32-33 to 43-32-36
south dakota.agency_name: South Dakota Department of Labor and Regulation, Division of Human Rights
south dakota.state_note: South Dakota is distinctive in explicitly covering psychiatric and mental disabilities in its public-access statute and in making it a criminal offense for a landlord to deny a service animal. Its 2018 housing law was an early anti-letter-mill law, and its 2026 misrepresentation law (SB 82) is new, so older guides that say South Dakota has no fake-service-animal penalty are out of date.
south dakota.sources: SDCL 20-13-23.2, SDCL 20-13-23.4, SDCL 22-35-9 (2026 SB 82, mylrc.sdlegislature.gov), SDCL 43-32-33 to 43-32-36, South Dakota Department of Labor and Regulation Division of Human Rights (dlr.sd.gov/human_rights/)

tennessee.service_animal_def: Tennessee uses different definitions by context. Public access (Tenn. Code Ann. 62-7-112) uses the older term 'dog guide' for a blind, physically disabled, or deaf or hard-of-hearing person led or accompanied by a dog guide. Housing (Tenn. Code Ann. 66-7-111) defines a service animal as a dog or miniature horse individually trained to work or perform tasks for a person with a disability. Criminal law (Tenn. Code Ann. 39-14-216) is broader, covering any animal individually trained or being trained to do work for a person with a physical, sensory, psychiatric, intellectual, or other mental disability.
tennessee.public_access_note: A proprietor of a place of public accommodation, amusement, or recreation — including inns, hotels, restaurants, stores, public conveyances, theaters, and public educational institutions — may not refuse entry to a person accompanied by a dog guide (Tenn. Code Ann. 62-7-112). The business may not require documentation such as proof the dog guide is certified, trained, or licensed, and may ask only the two ADA questions when the need is not obvious; the dog must be under the handler's control and may be removed only if out of control or not housebroken. Dog guides in training have public access when led by an employee or puppy raiser from a recognized training agency or school, wearing a harness and on a leash.
tennessee.esa_note: Emotional support animals are not service animals under the ADA and have no public-access rights in Tennessee; a 2024 law (Tenn. Code Ann. 68-14-729) expressly bars live animals whose sole function is comfort or emotional support from indoor areas of food service establishments, while trained service animals are excepted. In housing, Tennessee defines a 'support animal' (Tenn. Code Ann. 66-7-111) to include an animal prescribed or recommended by a health care provider to provide emotional support that alleviates identified symptoms of a disability.
tennessee.misrepresentation_penalty: Class B misdemeanor under Tenn. Code Ann. 39-16-304 for knowingly misrepresenting a service or support animal, including false claims or false documentation to a landlord or to an employee of a place of public accommodation. For misrepresentation of a service animal, the court must also impose 100 hours of community service to be completed within six months.
tennessee.housing_note: Under Tenn. Code Ann. 66-7-111 and 66-28-406, a tenant or prospective tenant with a disability may request an exception to a no-pets policy or pet fees for a service or support animal as a reasonable accommodation, with no extra payment for the animal. A landlord may request reliable documentation from a health care provider with actual knowledge of the disability; Tennessee's 2024 amendment bars documentation from websites whose primary function is selling ESA certificates, and landlords are not liable for injuries caused by a permitted service or support animal.
tennessee.state_statute: Tenn. Code Ann. 62-7-112 (public access, dog guides); Tenn. Code Ann. 66-7-111 and 66-28-406 (housing, service and support animals); Tenn. Code Ann. 39-16-304 (misrepresentation); Tenn. Code Ann. 68-14-729 (animals in food service establishments)
tennessee.legal_aid_name: Legal Aid Society of Middle Tennessee and the Cumberlands
tennessee.state_note: Tennessee is unusual in having three different service-animal definitions depending on whether the issue is public access, housing, or criminal law, and in expressly banning emotional support animals from indoor restaurant areas while giving them strong housing protection. Its 2024 anti-letter-mill provision and landlord liability shield are recent additions.
tennessee.sources: Tenn. Code Ann. 62-7-112, Tenn. Code Ann. 66-7-111, Tenn. Code Ann. 39-16-304, Tenn. Code Ann. 68-14-729, Tennessee Human Rights Commission (tn.gov/humanrights)

texas.service_animal_def: Texas defines a service animal (Tex. Hum. Res. Code 121.002) as a canine specially trained or equipped to do work or perform tasks for a person with a disability and used by a person with a disability — dogs only, with no miniature horses in the state definition. The statute's disability definition is broad and expressly includes mental or physical disabilities, intellectual or developmental disabilities, hearing or speech impairments, visual impairments, deafness, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and health conditions requiring special ambulatory devices. Animals in training have public access when with an approved trainer.
texas.public_access_note: A person with a disability who has or obtains an assistance animal is entitled to full and equal access to all public facilities, including streets, transportation, aircraft, lodging, government buildings, retail establishments, educational facilities, and food service locations (Tex. Hum. Res. Code 121.002 and 121.003), with no extra charge. A business may ask only the two ADA questions when the need is not obvious — whether the animal is required because of a disability, and what work or task it has been trained to perform — and may not demand proof of certification or training. Texas goes beyond the ADA by providing both criminal penalties and civil remedies for access denial, including a $300 minimum damages presumption.
texas.esa_note: Emotional support animals are not service animals under the ADA and have no public-access rights in Texas. Texas law uses the broader term 'assistance animal,' which includes an animal that provides emotional support alleviating medically identified symptoms of a disability, and that broader term is what gives housing protection — not public-access rights.
texas.misrepresentation_penalty: Misdemeanor under Tex. Hum. Res. Code 121.006, as strengthened by HB 4164 (2023): intentionally or knowingly representing that an animal is an assistance or service animal when it is not specially trained is punishable by a fine of not more than $1,000 and 30 hours of community service for a governmental entity or nonprofit serving persons with disabilities, to be completed within one year. Older sources citing a $300 maximum fine reflect the pre-2023 law.
texas.housing_note: A person with a disability who has or obtains an assistance animal is entitled to full and equal access to all housing accommodations and may not be required to pay extra compensation or make a deposit for the animal, though the person is liable for damage the animal does beyond reasonable wear and tear (Tex. Hum. Res. Code 121.003(h)). A landlord may ask for documentation of the disability-related need for an assistance animal where the need is not apparent.
texas.state_statute: Texas Human Resources Code Chapter 121 (Persons with Disabilities), especially Sections 121.002, 121.003, 121.004, and 121.006
texas.agency_name: Texas Workforce Commission, Civil Rights Division
texas.state_note: Texas has one of the most detailed state frameworks: it expressly names PTSD as a qualifying disability, gives service dogs in training public access, and has tiered felony penalties for harming a service animal — up to a third-degree felony for killing one (Tex. Penal Code 42.091). Its 2023 increase of the fake-service-animal fine from $300 to $1,000 is recent, so older guides understate the penalty.
texas.sources: Tex. Hum. Res. Code 121.002, 121.003, 121.006 (HB 4164, 2023), Tex. Penal Code 42.091, Texas Workforce Commission Civil Rights Division (twc.texas.gov)

utah.service_animal_def: Utah defines a service animal as any dog that is trained, or is in training, to do work or perform tasks for the benefit of an individual with a disability, including a physical, sensory, psychiatric, intellectual, or other mental disability, where the work or tasks are directly related to the disability (Utah Code 26B-6-802, formerly 62A-5b-102). The definition is limited to dogs — it excludes animals other than dogs, so miniature horses are not included in the state definition, though the ADA's miniature-horse provision still applies. Animals in training are expressly covered.
utah.public_access_note: A person with a disability accompanied by a service animal has the right to full and equal access to public places, including restaurants, stores, hotels, public transportation, and government buildings, with no extra charge. A business may ask only the two ADA questions when the need is not obvious — whether the animal is required because of a disability, and what work or task it has been trained to perform — and may not require proof of certification. Denying or interfering with that access is a class C misdemeanor, and trainers of service animals in training have the same public-access rights.
utah.esa_note: Emotional support animals are not service animals under the ADA and have no public-access rights in Utah. Utah law separately defines a 'support animal' for housing purposes as an animal that provides emotional support alleviating identified symptoms of a disability, and support animals are protected in housing as a reasonable accommodation, not in public places.
utah.misrepresentation_penalty: Class C misdemeanor under Utah Code 26B-6-805 (formerly 62A-5b-106) for intentionally and knowingly falsely representing that an animal is a service animal or support animal, knowingly misrepresenting a material fact to a health care provider to obtain documentation for that designation, or, for a person without a disability, using an animal to gain treatment or benefits provided only to a person with a disability. The statute section reviewed states no specific fine amount. Older sources calling this a class B misdemeanor reflect the pre-2019 law; HB 43 (2019) lowered it to class C.
utah.housing_note: In housing, a person with a disability may keep a service animal or support animal as a reasonable accommodation even in no-pets housing, with no pet deposit or extra fee for the animal. A landlord may request reliable documentation from a health care provider confirming the disability and the disability-related need if the need is not readily apparent, and knowingly providing false documentation is a class C misdemeanor.
utah.state_statute: Utah Code Title 26B, Chapter 6, Part 8, Rights and Privileges of an Individual with a Disability (formerly Title 62A, Chapter 5b), especially Sections 26B-6-802, 26B-6-803, and 26B-6-805
utah.agency_name: Utah Labor Commission, Utah Antidiscrimination and Labor Division (UALD)
utah.state_note: Utah's chapter was renumbered from Title 62A, Chapter 5b to Title 26B, Chapter 6, Part 8, so citations to 62A-5b-102 and 62A-5b-106 in older guides are the same law under new numbers. Utah is also distinctive in criminalizing false statements made to a health care provider to obtain service or support animal documentation, not just false claims made to a business or landlord.
utah.sources: Utah Code 26B-6-802, 26B-6-805 (formerly 62A-5b-102, 62A-5b-106, as amended by HB 43, 2019, le.utah.gov), Utah Labor Commission Antidiscrimination and Labor Division (laborcommission.utah.gov)

vermont.service_animal_def: Vermont's public-accommodations statute (9 V.S.A. 4502) uses the term 'service animal' without spelling out which species count in the statute itself. The Vermont Human Rights Commission's administrative rules define a service animal as any dog or miniature horse (meeting the qualifications in the rules) individually trained to do work or perform tasks that mitigate the limitations caused by the person's qualifying disability, including service dogs used by firefighters, law enforcement, and other rescue personnel. Individuals training an animal to perform as a service animal are expressly covered (9 V.S.A. 4502(b)(2)).
vermont.public_access_note: An owner or operator of a place of public accommodation — including schools, stores, restaurants, and other establishments offering goods or services to the general public — may not prohibit entry to a person with a disability accompanied by a service animal (9 V.S.A. 4502). A business may ask only the two ADA questions when the need is not obvious — whether the animal is required because of a disability, and what work or task it has been trained to perform — and may not require documentation, certification, a vest, or a harness. The animal must be under control and housebroken, and access may not be denied based on breed or size.
vermont.esa_note: Emotional support animals are not service animals under the ADA and have no public-access rights in Vermont, and Vermont has no ESA-specific public-access statute. Under the Human Rights Commission's rules, an assistance animal (including one providing emotional support) is permitted as a reasonable accommodation in housing but in places of public accommodation only at the entity's discretion.
vermont.misrepresentation_penalty: No specific state penalty — no Vermont statute reviewed sets a penalty for falsely claiming an animal is a service animal. General fraud or false-pretenses laws could still apply to fabricated documentation, and misrepresentation in housing could violate 9 V.S.A. 4503, but Vermont has no dedicated fake-service-animal statute.
vermont.housing_note: Under 9 V.S.A. 4503(a)(9), it is unlawful discrimination in the sale or rental of a dwelling to discriminate against a person because the person relies on specially trained animals, wheelchairs, or similar devices. A service animal or assistance animal must be allowed as a reasonable accommodation in housing, with no pet deposit or extra fee, and a landlord may ask for documentation of the disability-related need only where the need is not apparent.
vermont.state_statute: Vermont Fair Housing and Public Accommodations Act, 9 V.S.A. Chapter 139, especially 9 V.S.A. 4501, 4502, and 4503
vermont.state_note: Vermont is one of the more permissive states for service animals in training: 9 V.S.A. 4502(b)(2) expressly gives public-access rights to any individual training an animal to perform as a service animal, with no professional-trainer, harness, or identification condition stated in the statute. It is also one of the few states with no dedicated misrepresentation penalty at all.
vermont.sources: 9 V.S.A. 4501, 4502, 4503, Vermont Human Rights Commission Administrative Rules and FAQ (hrc.vermont.gov)

virginia.service_animal_def: Virginia defines a 'service dog' (Va. Code 51.5-40.1) as a dog trained to do work or perform tasks for the benefit of a mobility-impaired or otherwise disabled person, where the work or tasks are directly related to the individual's disability or disorder — including guiding, pulling a wheelchair, assisting during a seizure, alerting to allergens, retrieving or carrying items, and providing physical support and assistance with balance. Emotional support, well-being, comfort, or companionship does not count as work or tasks. Virginia covers guide dogs, hearing dogs, and service dogs, all dogs only, and dogs in training at least six months old are covered (Va. Code 51.5-44(E)).
virginia.public_access_note: A person with a disability has the right to be accompanied by a trained guide dog, hearing dog, or service dog in the public places and accommodations listed in Va. Code 51.5-44(B), including public conveyances, hotels, restaurants, stores, theaters, and government buildings, with no extra charge, though the handler is liable for damage the dog causes. A business may ask only the two ADA questions when the need is not obvious, and may not require certification; a hearing dog is identified by a blaze orange leash and a service dog by a harness, backpack, or vest identifying it. Virginia goes beyond the ADA by extending access to dogs in training at least six months old.
virginia.esa_note: Emotional support animals are not service animals under the ADA or Virginia law — Virginia expressly excludes emotional support, well-being, comfort, or companionship from the definition of work or tasks — and they have no public-access rights. In housing, an emotional support animal may qualify as an assistance animal and be allowed as a reasonable accommodation under the Virginia Fair Housing Law, with documentation of the disability-related need where the need is not apparent.
virginia.misrepresentation_penalty: Class 4 misdemeanor under Va. Code 51.5-44.1 for knowingly and willfully fitting a dog with a harness, collar, vest, or sign, or using an identification card commonly used by a person with a disability, in order to represent that the dog is a service dog or hearing dog to fraudulently gain public access under Va. Code 51.5-44.
virginia.housing_note: Under the Virginia Fair Housing Law, a housing provider must allow a service dog or other assistance animal as a reasonable accommodation for a person with a disability, with no pet deposit or extra fee for the animal, and the handler is liable for damage the animal causes. A provider may request documentation confirming the disability-related need where the disability or need is not readily apparent.
virginia.state_statute: Code of Virginia Title 51.5, Chapter 9, Rights of Persons with Disabilities, especially Va. Code 51.5-40.1, 51.5-44, and 51.5-44.1
virginia.agency_name: Office of Civil Rights, Office of the Attorney General of Virginia
virginia.state_note: Virginia is distinctive in requiring visible identification for its service dogs — a harness, backpack, or vest for a service dog and a blaze orange leash for a hearing dog — while still requiring no certification or state registration, and in covering dogs in training as young as six months old. Virginia has no separate human rights commission; disability discrimination complaints go to the Attorney General's Office of Civil Rights.
virginia.sources: Va. Code 51.5-40.1, 51.5-44, 51.5-44.1 (law.lis.virginia.gov), Virginia Office of the Attorney General, Office of Civil Rights (oag.state.va.us/citizen-resources/civil-rights)

washington.service_animal_def: Washington defines a service animal (RCW 49.60.040) as any dog or miniature horse individually trained to do work or perform tasks for the benefit of an individual with a disability, including a physical, sensory, psychiatric, intellectual, or other mental disability, where the work or tasks are directly related to the disability. A 2024 amendment (SB 5788) added definitions for a 'service animal trainee' — any dog or miniature horse undergoing training to become a service animal — and a 'service animal trainer.' Washington's broader disability definition covers sensory, mental, or physical impairments that are medically cognizable or exist as a record or perception.
